## Definition

Use the flat oriented, time-oriented affine Minkowski model, signature $(-,+,+,+)$, and SI convention $x^0=ct$ of [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. A **relativistic-particle-mechanics collision configuration** is a mass-specified causal collision datum of [[def-sr-collision-datum-and-conservation]]: an event $p\in A$, a finite nonempty incoming list $P_1,\ldots,P_N\in V$, and a finite nonempty outgoing list $P'_1,\ldots,P'_K\in V$, where every leg is a nonzero future-causal vector in the same displacement space $V$. A massive leg has a recorded mass $m>0$ and the massive-sector momentum of [[def-rpm-mechanical-momentum-and-observer-energy]]; a null leg has recorded mass $0$ and is a nonzero future-null vector with its scale specified independently. The definition does not identify a null momentum with $mU$ at $m=0$.

The side totals are the finite vector sums $Q_{\rm in}:=\sum_{i=1}^N P_i$ and $Q_{\rm out}:=\sum_{j=1}^K P'_j$. All legs are attached to the same event, so the sums compare vectors in one affine displacement space; no transport between different events is part of the datum. The adjective **isolated** is reserved for a model condition used by the postulate below: no external four-momentum transfer during the idealized event and no omitted incoming or outgoing leg.

At an event, an **observer** is a future unit timelike vector $n$ with $\eta(n,n)=-1$, and its rest space is $n^\perp=\{v\in V:\eta(v,n)=0\}$, as in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. Observer energy $E_n(P):=-c\eta(P,n)$ and spatial momentum $q_n(P):=P+\eta(P,n)n\in n^\perp$ are those of [[def-rpm-mechanical-momentum-and-observer-energy]]. Their units are joules and kilogram metres per second. An inertial laboratory means one named inertial chart and its time-axis observer; it is not a general observer congruence or an arbitrary coordinate chart.

## Definition

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Fix a prescribed smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold $(M,g,T)$ with signature $(-+++)$, as in [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Here $T$ denotes the supplied smooth timelike field selecting the future cone, called $N$ in that geometric definition. Use the distinction among a spacetime, a worldline, a pointwise observer, an observer congruence, a tetrad and a chart given in [[def-rpm-spacetime-observer-and-worldline]]. This definition does not make $g$ dynamical.

At each $x\in M$, define $v^\flat:=g_x(v,\cdot)$ for $v\in T_xM$. Nondegeneracy of $g_x$ makes $\flat_x:T_xM\to T_x^*M$ an isomorphism; write $p^\sharp:=\flat_x^{-1}(p)$ for $p\in T_x^*M$, and define $g_x^{-1}(p,r):=g_x(p^\sharp,r^\sharp)$. In a chart, if $g_{ab}:=g(\partial_a,\partial_b)$ and $(g^{ab})$ is its inverse matrix, then $p^\sharp=\sum_{a,b=0}^3g^{ab}p_b\partial_a$. A covector $p$ is **future causal** here exactly when $p^\sharp$ is a nonzero future-causal vector in the sense of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]].

In this relativistic-particle model, $m>0$ is a fixed **primitive mass parameter** measured in kilograms, and $c>0$ is a fixed **primitive conversion parameter** measured in metres per second. They are parameters of the adopted physical formulation, not quantities derived by this definition. Coordinates $x^a$ in an SI chart have length units; a cotangent vector $p=p_a\,dx^a$ has units of momentum, $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$, when all four coordinates are in metres. The canonical one-form $p_a\,dx^a$ therefore has action units $\mathrm{J\,s}$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be a $C^1$ curve; let $\lambda$ be its real parameter and write $V=d\gamma/d\lambda$. When $V$ is future timelike, set $s:=\sqrt{-g(V,V)}$ and define the proper-time density by $d\tau=s\,d\lambda/c$. The tangent is then nonzero. If $\widetilde\lambda=f(\lambda)$ is an increasing $C^1$ reparametrization with $f'(\lambda)>0$, then $s_{\widetilde\lambda}=s_\lambda/f'(\lambda)$, so $s_{\widetilde\lambda}\,d\widetilde\lambda=s_\lambda\,d\lambda$. The length action $-mc\int s\,d\lambda$ has action units. For a future unit observer $n$ and future causal covector $p$, define the model normal-observer energy and spatial momentum covector by

$$E_n(p):=-c\,p(n),\qquad q_n(p):=p+p(n)n^\flat,$$

where $n^\flat=g(n,\cdot)$. We have $q_n(p)(n)=0$; write $n^\perp:=\{v\in T_xM:g_x(v,n)=0\}$. To verify the norm convention, choose a $g_x$-orthonormal basis $(e_0,e_1,e_2,e_3)$ with $e_0$ future-directed (replace $e_0$ by $-e_0$ if necessary), and write $n=n^0e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3n^ie_i$ and $v=v^0e_0+\sum_{i=1}^3v^ie_i$. Use $n_s\cdot v_s:=\sum_{i=1}^3n^iv^i$, $|n_s|^2:=\sum_{i=1}^3(n^i)^2$, and $|v_s|^2:=\sum_{i=1}^3(v^i)^2$. The future-cone convention gives $n^0>|n_s|$, and $g_x(n,n)=-1$ gives $(n^0)^2=1+|n_s|^2$. If $g_x(v,n)=0$, then $v^0=(n_s\cdot v_s)/n^0$, so

$$g_x(v,v)=|v_s|^2-\frac{(n_s\cdot v_s)^2}{(n^0)^2}\ge\frac{|v_s|^2}{(n^0)^2}.$$

Here $|n_s|^2|v_s|^2-(n_s\cdot v_s)^2=\sum_{1\le i<j\le3}(n^iv^j-n^jv^i)^2\ge0$; if $v_s=0$, orthogonality also gives $v^0=0$. Thus $g_x$ is positive definite on $n^\perp$, and the isomorphism $\sharp_x$ carries covectors annihilating $n$ onto $n^\perp$, so $g_x^{-1}$ is positive definite on that covector subspace. Define $\|q_n(p)\|_n:=\sqrt{g_x^{-1}(q_n(p),q_n(p))}$. These are quantity definitions and unit conventions; they do not identify canonical momentum with mechanical momentum, assert that an apparatus measured these values, or establish a dynamical law.

## Definition

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as in [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. Let $(P,\omega)$ be a smooth symplectic manifold. For every smooth real function $F$ on an open set $U\subseteq P$, define its Hamiltonian vector field $X_F$ by $\omega_z(X_F(z),v)=dF_z(v)$ for every $z\in U$ and $v\in T_zP$, and define $\{F,G\}:=dF(X_G)$. Nondegeneracy of $\omega$ makes $X_F$ unique; in local coordinates its coefficients are obtained by inverting the smooth nonsingular matrix of $\omega$, so $X_F$ and the bracket are smooth. Let $\chi_1,\ldots,\chi_r\in C^\infty(U,\mathbb R)$ be a regular constraint family on the common zero surface $N=\{z\in U:\chi_a(z)=0\text{ for all }a\}$ as defined by [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]: the differentials $d\chi_a$ are linearly independent at every point of $N$. The family is **first-class on $N$** when

$$\{\chi_a,\chi_b\}(z)=0\qquad\text{for every }z\in N\text{ and all }a,b.$$

Equivalently, each pairwise bracket is weakly zero in the notation $F\approx0$ of [[def-rpm-h-regular-constraint-system]]. On a canonical cotangent phase space this intrinsic convention agrees with [[thm-rpm-h-canonical-poisson-and-flow]]: $\{F,G\}=F_{q^i}G_{p_i}-F_{p_i}G_{q^i}$. This definition is a pointwise closure condition on the stated regular surface; it does not assert multiplier-algorithm termination or global quotient regularity.

## Definition

Assume countable choice ACω, as in [[def-countable-choice]], for the smooth cotangent-bundle carrier convention used by this page; no full Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $(M,g,T)$ be a smooth, time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-+++)$, with the geometric meaning fixed by [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]]. Here $T$ denotes the future-cone field called $N$ in that definition. Let $I\subset\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^3$ be open, and let $U\subset M$ be open. A **temporal product chart** is a smooth diffeomorphism $\chi:U\to I\times\Omega$. Its coordinate functions $x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3$ are the four component functions of $\chi$. Spatial indices $i,j$ range over $1,2,3$, spacetime indices $a,b$ range over $0,1,2,3$, and repeated upper/lower indices are summed. We require $x^0$ and each $x^i$ to have length units in the physical interpretation.

The chart has **lapse-shift data** $(N,\beta,h)$ when $N:I\times\Omega\to(0,\infty)$, $\beta^i:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and $h_{ij}:I\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, $h_{ij}=h_{ji}$, and the matrix $(h_{ij})$ is positive definite at each point, with

$$g=-N^2(dx^0)^2+h_{ij}(dx^i+\beta^i dx^0)(dx^j+\beta^j dx^0).$$

Write $h^{ij}$ for the inverse matrix. The normal field is

$$n=N^{-1}(\partial_0-\beta^i\partial_i).$$

Direct contraction gives $g(n,n)=-1$; require that $n$ is future-directed in the supplied time orientation. This field of observers is distinct from the coordinate vector $\partial_0$, which may be spacelike. The coefficients $N,\beta^i,h_{ij}$ are dimensionless when all four coordinates are in metres. This definition is local to the specified product chart; it asserts no global temporal foliation.

## Definition

Let $m,c,\kappa>0$, let $x,p\in\mathbb R^3$, and set

$$D:=(\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\})\times\mathbb R^3,\qquad r:=|x|,\qquad \mathcal E(p):=\sqrt{m^2c^4+c^2|p|^2}.$$

The **repulsive relativistic Coulomb Hamiltonian** is

$$H(x,p):=\mathcal E(p)+\frac{\kappa}{r},$$

and its **phase system** is the autonomous ODE on the open set $D$

$$\dot x=\nabla_pH=\frac{c^2p}{\mathcal E(p)},\qquad \dot p=-\nabla_xH=\frac{\kappa x}{r^3}.$$

Here the system parameter $t$ is time in seconds and dot denotes $d/dt$; $m$ is a positive mass parameter (kilograms in the SI interpretation), $c$ a positive speed parameter (metres per second), and $\kappa$ a positive energy-times-length parameter (joule-metres). Define the radial momentum $p_r:=x\cdot p/r$ and angular-momentum vector $J:=x\times p$. A trajectory is a $C^1$ map $z=(x,p):I\to D$ on a real interval $I$ with nonempty interior, satisfying this ODE in the interval-solution sense of [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A trajectory $\widetilde z:\widetilde I\to D$ **extends** $z$ if $I\subseteq\widetilde I$ and $\widetilde z|_I=z$; it is a **proper extension** if $I\subsetneq\widetilde I$. A trajectory is **maximal** if it has no proper extension as a solution of this same system in $D$. This definition alone asserts neither existence nor uniqueness of maximal trajectories.

This is only a mathematical phase system. Its physical interpretation as a charged particle in an externally prescribed Coulomb field requires separate model assumptions.

## Definition

Assume AC. If $P$ and $Q$ are probability measures on the same measurable space, define
$$D(P\Vert Q)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int h\log h\,dQ,&P\ll Q\text{ and }h=dP/dQ,\\+\infty,&P\not\ll Q.\end{cases}$$
Use $0\log0=0$. The Radon–Nikodym derivative $h$ is unique up to $Q$-almost-everywhere equality, so the integral is independent of its representative. Its negative part is finite because $-u\log u\leq1/e$ for $0\leq u\leq1$ and $Q$ is a probability; hence $D(P\Vert Q)$ is a well-defined extended real number.

## Statement

Let $C=[0,1)^d$ for an integer $d\geq1$. Let $\mathsf C_f(C)$ be the set of finite subsets of $C$, represented by their cardinality $n$ and their uniquely lexicographically increasing list $(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. Give this set the Borel structure of the countable disjoint union of the Borel subspaces of $C^n$ consisting of strictly increasing lists. For each Borel $B\subseteq C$, let $N_B(\eta)=\#(\eta\cap B)$. Then
$$\mathcal B(\mathsf C_f(C))=\sigma\{N_B:B\in\mathcal B(C)\}.$$

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite simple configurations and sorted-list Borel structure in the Statement.

[F1] Finite products carry the product sigma-algebra generated by measurable rectangles, and finite products of standard Borel spaces are standard Borel ([[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]], [[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], [[def-standard-borel-space]], [[lem-finite-products-of-standard-borel-spaces-are-standard-borel]]).

[F2] A pi-system generating a sigma-algebra determines every lambda-system containing it ([[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]).

[F3] Use the left-closed, right-open dyadic intervals $I_{m,k}=[k2^{-m},(k+1)2^{-m})$, $0\le k<2^m$. The natural/integer indices and integer powers are those of [[def-natural-numbers]], [[def-integers]], and [[def-integer-power]]; their Borel and partition properties are proved locally below, rather than attributed to a supplier with the opposite face convention.

## Proof

**Given:** $d\geq1$ and the finite configurations in the Statement.

1.1 On the component of configurations with exactly $n$ points, $N_B(x_1,\ldots,x_n)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf1_B(x_j)$ is Borel for every Borel $B\subseteq C$. The count of $C$ identifies the component $n$, so every count map is Borel on the full disjoint union. Thus the count-generated sigma-algebra is contained in the sorted-list Borel sigma-algebra. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Each $I_{m,k}$ is Borel as the intersection of a closed ray and an open ray. Distinct interval interiors are disjoint and an adjacent endpoint belongs only to the interval beginning there. Induction on the number of adjacent intervals gives $\bigcup_{k<j}I_{m,k}=[0,j2^{-m})$; at $j=2^m$ this is $[0,1)$. Thus they partition the reference interval. Each interval is the union of its two intervals at the next level, so the partition refines and its mesh tends to zero. Cartesian products give the corresponding Borel partitions of $C$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Let $(T,\mathcal T)$ be any measurable space. For $H\in\mathcal B(C)\otimes\mathcal T$, define $M_H(\eta,t)=\sum_{x\in\eta}\mathbf1_H(x,t)$. The class of such $H$ for which $M_H$ is measurable with respect to the count sigma-algebra times $\mathcal T$ contains every rectangle $A\times D$, since $M_{A\times D}(\eta,t)=N_A(\eta)\mathbf1_D(t)$. It is closed under relative complements because $M_{(C\times T)\setminus H}=N_C-M_H$, and under disjoint countable unions by pointwise convergence of finite partial sums. Rectangles form a generating pi-system, so [F2] proves measurability for every product-measurable $H$. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Fix a component with $n$ distinct points and an index $k\leq n$. Recover the coordinates of the $k$th lexicographic point recursively. Initially the selected prefix is empty and its rank is $r=k$. At coordinate $j$, with measurable prefix $p=(a_1,\ldots,a_{j-1})$, use step 2.1 on the Borel set $H_j=\{(x,p,t):x_\ell=p_\ell\ (\ell<j),\ x_j<t\}$, where $t\in[0,1]$. For each dyadic interval $I=[u,v)$ in coordinate $j$, the number of points matching the prefix and having $x_j\in I$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,v)-M_{H_j}(\eta,p,u)$, hence is measurable. The interval containing the $r$th such coordinate is the first whose cumulative count reaches $r$; the nested interval closures have diameters tending to zero, so their left endpoints converge to that coordinate $a_j$. The count of matching points with $x_j<a_j$ is $M_{H_j}(\eta,p,a_j)$, measurable by step 2.1 after composition with the measurable prefix and $a_j$. Subtracting it from $r$ gives the positive rank among points with the extended prefix. [F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, construct]

4.1 The recursive choice in step 3.1 is the usual lexicographic ordering rule: among points with a fixed prefix, sort by the next coordinate, retain the value at the current rank, then subtract the points strictly below it to obtain the rank among ties. After coordinate $d$, distinctness leaves exactly one point, namely $x_k$. Thus all coordinate functions of every sorted point are count-measurable. The Borel sigma-algebra on the sorted-list component is generated by its coordinate maps, so it is contained in the count-generated sigma-algebra there. [step 3.1, F1]

5.1 The count $N_C$ partitions the full configuration space into its countable components. Applying step 4.1 on each component shows that every sorted-list Borel set is count-measurable; step 1.1 proves the reverse inclusion. The displayed sigma-algebra equality follows. [step 1.1, step 4.1, F1] ∎

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice and fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^d$, let $C_i=i+[0,1)^d$. These are left-closed, right-open cells. For every $x\in\mathbb R^d$, [[lem-integer-part]] supplies the unique integers $i_j$ with $i_j\le x_j<i_j+1$, so $x$ belongs to exactly one $C_i$. The cells are Borel products of closed/open ray intersections and have volume one by [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]], whose statement covers this face convention. A finite configuration in $C_i$ is a finite subset of distinct points. Encode it by its cardinality $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and its uniquely lexicographically increasing list of local coordinates $(x_1-i,\ldots,x_n-i)\in([0,1)^d)^n$. Pad the code after its first $n$ coordinates with the zero vector. For fixed $n$, the strictly increasing lists form a Borel subset of $([0,1]^d)^n$, since lexicographic strict order is a finite union of coordinate-equality and coordinate-inequality conditions. Thus all codes form a Borel subset of $\mathbb N_0\times([0,1]^d)^{\mathbb N}$. Each factor $[0,1]^d$ is Polish as a closed subspace of complete $\mathbb R^d$ with a countable dense rational grid; $\mathbb N_0$ with its discrete metric is Polish. The ambient space is Polish by [[cor-countable-products-and-g-delta-subspaces-of-polish-spaces-are-polish]] (and is completely metrized by [[lem-standard-complete-metric-on-a-countable-product]]), so [[lem-borel-subspaces-admit-polish-presentations]] makes the cell space $E_i$ standard Borel. By [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]], its sigma-algebra is generated by the counts $N_B$ for Borel $B\subseteq C_i$.

Use $e^t:=\exp(t)$ for real $t$, with $\exp$ defined by [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]; for a real measurable function $f$, $e^f$ means the pointwise composition $\exp\circ f$. For $\lambda>0$, give a cell configuration with $n$ points probability $\exp(-\lambda)\lambda^n/n!$ for its count. The probabilities sum to $\exp(-\lambda)\exp(\lambda)=\exp(0)=1$ by the exponential power series and [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]. Conditional on count $n$, take the $n$-fold product of normalized Lebesgue measure on $C_i$, restrict it to the complement of the collision diagonals, and push it forward by lexicographic sorting. The product exists by the finite product-measure theorem; each collision diagonal is null by Tonelli and the fact that Lebesgue measure gives every singleton measure zero, so the restricted measure still has mass one. Sorting is Borel on the finitely many permutation regions of the no-collision set. This defines a law $\pi_{i,\lambda}$ on $E_i$; for $n=0$, use the empty product and the empty configuration. Let $\Omega=\prod_{i\in\mathbb Z^d}E_i$ with its product cylinder sigma-algebra. The product sigma-algebra is generated by the cell-coordinate sigma-algebras, each generated by counts on Borel subsets of its bounded cell by [[lem-tdmath-counts-generate-configuration-sigma]]. Conversely every bounded-region count is a finite sum of these cell counts, since a bounded set meets finitely many cells. Thus the product cylinder sigma-algebra is exactly the sigma-algebra generated by all bounded-Borel count maps. For each $\lambda>0$, $Q_\lambda$ denotes the unique probability on $\Omega$ whose finite cell marginals are the products of the corresponding $\pi_{i,\lambda}$. Existence and uniqueness follow from [[thm-kolmogorov-extension-for-standard-borel-coordinate-spaces]]. In particular every translation $T_x$ is measurable since $N_A(T_x\omega)=N_{A-x}(\omega)$. The unit-intensity reference is $Q:=Q_1$.

Identify each $\omega\in\Omega$ with the simple locally finite counting measure obtained by uniting its finite cell configurations. For a bounded Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, write $N_A(\omega)=\omega(A)$ and $|A|$ for its Lebesgue measure. Define translation by $T_x\omega(A)=\omega(A-x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R^d$. The next item proves that under $Q_\lambda$, counts in disjoint bounded Borel sets are independent Poisson random variables with means $\lambda|A|$ and that $Q_\lambda$ is translation invariant. This item is a mathematical reference construction and makes no physical claim.

## Definition

Assume AC. Fix an integer dimension $d\geq1$, use the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|_2$ from [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], define $|x|_\infty=\max_j|x_j|$, and use the numerical coordinate conventions in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]]. A finite configuration is a finite subset $\omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ with no repeated points; its number of points is $N(\omega)$. A pair potential is an even Borel function, measurable for the Borel sigma-algebra generated by open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]), $\phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where even means $\phi(-x)=\phi(x)$. Define
$$H_\phi(\omega)=\sum_{\{x,y\}\subset\omega}\phi(x-y),\qquad H_\phi(\varnothing)=0.$$
The sum is over unordered two-point subsets, so every term is evaluated at a nonzero separation; if any term is $+\infty$, the sum is $+\infty$.

The potential is stable if some $B\geq0$ satisfies $H_\phi(\omega)\geq-BN(\omega)$ for every finite configuration. It is superstable in the Georgii splitting convention if $\phi=\phi_s+\phi_r$, where $\phi_s$ is stable and $\phi_r\geq0$ everywhere and, for some $r_0,\delta>0$, $\phi_r(x)\geq\delta$ whenever $|x|_\infty\leq r_0$. It is lower regular if a nonnegative nonincreasing $\psi:[0,\infty)\to[0,+\infty]$ satisfies
$$\phi(x)\geq-\psi(|x|_\infty),\qquad \int_0^\infty\psi(r)r^{d-1}\,dr<\infty.$$
It is regular if it is lower regular and, for some $R<\infty$, $\phi(x)\leq\psi(|x|_\infty)$ whenever $|x|_\infty\geq R$. These are the conventions used for the interacting results on this page. A genuine divergent positive core is the separate additional condition that some nonincreasing $\chi:(0,r_1]\to(0,\infty)$ satisfies $\phi(x)\geq\chi(|x|_\infty)$ for $0<|x|_\infty\leq r_1$ and $\int_0^{r_1}\chi(r)r^{d-1}dr=+\infty$; it is not implied by superstability.

For $L>0$ put $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$, $V_L=L^d$, and let $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ be $H_\phi$ for configurations restricted to $\Lambda_L$. For a regular potential and sufficiently large periodic cubes, periodize $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$ by $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and set
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x}\phi(y-x),$$
interpreting the value as $+\infty$ if a positive infinite term occurs. Under this regularity hypothesis, the far image sum is absolutely convergent for all sufficiently large $L$ by [[lem-tdmath-integrable-tail-diagonal-gap]]; this is the image convention used below. With fixed numerical length and energy units, the canonical positional partition is
$$Z(L,N;\beta)=\frac1{N!}\int_{\Lambda_L^N}e^{-\beta H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N)}dq_1\cdots dq_N,\quad Z(L,0;\beta)=1,$$
where the tuple notation means $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=H_\phi(\{q_1,\ldots,q_N\})$ when the coordinates are distinct, and $H_\phi(q_1,\ldots,q_N):=+\infty$ on collision diagonals. The integrand is therefore zero on collisions; these diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero by the no-collision construction in [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], so this convention leaves all partition integrals unchanged. For $N=0$ the empty tuple has energy zero. Here $\beta>0$, and the grand partition is $\Xi(L;a,\beta)=\sum_{N\geq0}a^NZ(L,N;\beta)$ for numerical activity $a>0$. The normalized unit-intensity Poisson version is $Z_Q(L;z,\beta)=E_{Q_{\Lambda_L}}[z^{N_{\Lambda_L}}e^{-\beta H_{L,\mathrm{free}}}]$; since the Poisson density contributes $e^{-V_L}$, $\Xi(L;z,\beta)=e^{V_L}Z_Q(L;z,\beta)$. A physical pressure identification is not part of this mathematical definition.

For a probability law $P$ on the configuration space of [[def-tdmath-poisson-configuration-reference]], stationarity means $P\circ T_x^{-1}=P$ for every $x\in\mathbb R^d$. When $P$ is stationary and $E_PN_{[0,1)^d}<\infty$ (finite intensity), write $\rho(P)=E_PN_{[0,1)^d}$. Use the finite-region relative entropy $D$ defined in [[def-tdmath-finite-region-relative-entropy]]. If $\phi$ is stable with constant $B$, then $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}\geq-BN_{\Lambda_L}$, so the negative part of $H_{L,\mathrm{free}}$ is $P$-integrable for every such $P$. Whenever the limit exists, write
$$\mathcal E(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}E_PH_{L,\mathrm{free}},\qquad I(P)=\lim_{L\to\infty}V_L^{-1}D(P_{\Lambda_L}\Vert Q_{\Lambda_L}).$$
In the variational results below, $\Phi(P)$ denotes this same positional energy density: $\Phi(P):=\mathcal E(P)$. The cited results establish existence under their stated hypotheses; this definition does not assume either limit exists for every stationary finite-intensity law.

## Definition

Fix an integer spatial dimension $d\geq1$, a reference length $\ell_0>0$ measured in metres, and a bounded Lebesgue-measurable region $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ with dimensionless volume $V=|\Lambda|<\infty$. Its physical region is $\ell_0\Lambda$. The coordinate $x\in\Lambda$ is dimensionless and represents physical position $\ell_0x$. Use the Euclidean norm $|x|_2=(\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2)^{1/2}$ and the maximum norm $|x|_\infty=\max_{1\leq j\leq d}|x_j|$. A finite positional configuration of $N$ classical point particles in $\Lambda$ is an unordered simple set $\omega=\{x_1,\ldots,x_N\}\subset\Lambda$; simple means that no point is repeated. Particle number $N$ is a dimensionless nonnegative integer. When $V>0$, the physical number density corresponding to the dimensionless density $N/V$ is $N/(\ell_0^dV)$, in $\mathrm{m}^{-d}$; no density $N/V$ is assigned when $V=0$.

A pair potential is an even measurable function $\varphi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$, where $\varphi(x)$ is the interaction energy in joules at physical displacement $\ell_0x$ and evenness means $\varphi(x)=\varphi(-x)$. Set $E_0=1\,\mathrm J$ and $\widehat\varphi=\varphi/E_0$. Whenever $\widehat\varphi$ is Borel measurable, it is the dimensionless numerical potential used by [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]. For a labelled representative of $\omega$, define the positional pair energy
$$H_N(\omega)=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\varphi(x_i-x_j),\qquad H_0=H_1=0.$$
If any pair is forbidden by the potential, its energy and hence $H_N$ are $+\infty$. This model contains no kinetic energy, internal molecular coordinates, quantum exchange terms, or external field.

The interaction is stable if there is a constant $B\geq0$, measured in joules, such that $H_N(\omega)\geq-BN$ for every finite simple configuration. It has a regular integrable tail if there are $R>0$ and a nonnegative nonincreasing measurable function $\psi:[R,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$, measured in joules, such that $|\varphi(x)|\leq\psi(|x|_2)$ for $|x|_2\geq R$ and
$$\int_R^\infty r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr<\infty.$$
A stable potential with this tail condition is the stable regularly tempered class used for the free-cube results on this page. Superstability and a positive divergent core are stronger, separate hypotheses and are not implied by stability.

At temperature $T>0$ measured in kelvins, use the exact SI Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm B}=1.380649\times10^{-23}\,\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$ of [[def-td-si-quantities]] and write $\beta=(k_{\mathrm B}T)^{-1}$ in joules inverse. Thus $\beta H_N$ is dimensionless. Pass the dimensionless numerical inverse temperature $\widehat\beta=E_0\beta=E_0/(k_{\mathrm B}T)$ and numerical energy $\widehat H_N=H_N/E_0$ to the mathematical partition definitions of [[def-tdmath-superstable-regular-interaction]]; for finite energies, $\widehat\beta\widehat H_N=\beta H_N$. For the periodic energy defined below, use the same conversion $\widehat H_{L,\mathrm{per}}=H_{L,\mathrm{per}}/E_0$. Infinite-energy configurations receive zero positive-temperature weight without evaluating $\beta(+\infty)$. The activity $z>0$ is dimensionless relative to the reference intensity $\ell_0^{-d}$. A free-wall finite-volume model contains only positions in $\Lambda$ and uses $H_N$ above.

For periodic boundary conditions, identify a cubic cell of side $L$ in these dimensionless coordinates with the torus $\mathbb R^d/(L\mathbb Z^d)$. For its half-open representative $\Lambda_L=[0,L)^d$ and a finite simple configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_L$, define the periodic continuation $\omega^{\mathrm{per}}=\{x+Lk:x\in\omega,\ k\in\mathbb Z^d\}$ and
$$H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=\frac12\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{\substack{y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}}\\ y\ne x}}\varphi(y-x).$$
Here the inner sum omits only the identical point $y=x$; it includes images of the same particle in other cells. The factor $1/2$ removes double counting of ordered representatives of each periodic pair. For any fixed $L>0$ and finite $\omega$, the $|k|_\infty=m$ image shell has $O_d(m^{d-1})$ terms and, outside finitely many $m$, $|y-x+Lk|_2\geq (L/2)m$. Monotonicity and the finite weighted tail integral imply $\sum_m m^{d-1}\psi(Lm/2)<\infty$, so the far-image tail is absolutely convergent. The remaining near-image set is finite; a term $+\infty$ makes $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}=+\infty$, and otherwise the finite near terms plus the absolutely convergent tail define the sum. Translating a centered half-open cell to $[0,L)^d$ preserves every displacement and this energy. Free-wall and periodic preparations are distinct boundary conditions. All limits on this page concern positional configurations and do not by themselves include a momentum integral or a full phase-space energy shell.

## Definition

Use the dimensionless coordinates, simple configurations, and pair potential of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], with $d\geq2$ as stated in this physical scope. The boundary $\partial\Lambda$ is the topological boundary in the Euclidean topology of $\mathbb R^d$, and $\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda)=\inf_{y\in\partial\Lambda}|x-y|_2$. For a bounded measurable region $\Lambda$, define its two-sided layer of width $s>0$ by
$$\partial_s\Lambda=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{dist}(x,\partial\Lambda)\leq s\}.$$
A sequence $(\Lambda_k)_{k\geq1}$ of bounded measurable regions is van Hove if $0<|\Lambda_k|<\infty$, $|\Lambda_k|\to\infty$, and, for every fixed $s>0$,
$$\frac{|\partial_s\Lambda_k|}{|\Lambda_k|}\longrightarrow0.$$
This is the two-sided Euclidean boundary-layer condition used by the mathematical shape suppliers; it controls points on both sides of $\partial\Lambda_k$. Increasing volume alone does not imply it. A free wall permits particles only in $\Lambda_k$ and includes no exterior particles. A periodic wall uses the specified periodic cell and its image convention.

For the deterministic exterior class, let $C=[-1/2,1/2)^d$ and $\Lambda_n=[-n-1/2,n+1/2)^d$, with dimensionless volume $V_n=|\Lambda_n|$. A configuration $\zeta\subset\mathbb R^d$ is locally finite if $|\zeta\cap K|<\infty$ for every bounded set $K\subset\mathbb R^d$. For such $\zeta$, write $N_{C+i}(\zeta)=|\zeta\cap(C+i)|$. The parameter $t$ is dimensionless. Given $0\leq t<\infty$, define
$$\Omega(t)=\left\{\zeta:\sum_{i\in\Lambda_n\cap\mathbb Z^d}N_{C+i}(\zeta)^2\leq tV_n\ \text{for every integer }n\geq0\right\}.$$
For an interior finite configuration $\omega\subset\Lambda_n$ and $\zeta\in\Omega(t)$, its exterior interaction is
$$W_n(\omega,\zeta)=\sum_{x\in\omega}\sum_{y\in\zeta\setminus\Lambda_n}\varphi(x-y).$$
This sum is well-defined in $\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$. Indeed, Cauchy--Schwarz and the defining bound for $\Omega(t)$ give $|\zeta\cap\Lambda_m|\leq\sqrt t\,V_m=O_t(m^d)$. Since $\omega$ is finite and bounded, for each fixed $x\in\omega$ and all sufficiently large dyadic shells $2^k\leq |y|_2<2^{k+1}$, one has $|x-y|_2\geq c2^k$ for some $c>0$. The absolute interaction on that shell is at most a constant times $2^{kd}\psi(c2^k)$. These bounds are summable: monotonicity gives $\int_{c2^{k-1}}^{c2^k}r^{d-1}\psi(r)\,dr\geq C_d2^{kd}\psi(c2^k)$ for a constant $C_d>0$, and the tail integral is finite. Only finitely many near exterior points remain; if one contributes $+\infty$, set $W_n=+\infty$, and otherwise the near sum and absolutely convergent tail define $W_n$. A positive infinite value has zero Boltzmann weight. The class $\Omega(t)$ is a fixed uniform bound on exterior cell counts, not permission for an arbitrary volume-filling external potential. The van Hove and uniformly tempered exterior conditions are separate boundary regimes.

## Postulate

Let $\Lambda\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded Lebesgue-measurable region in the dimensionless coordinates of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. Use the completed product-Lebesgue sigma-algebra on $\Lambda^N$. For $N\geq1$, let
$$D_{\Lambda,N}=\{(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in\Lambda^N:x_i\ne x_j\text{ whenever }i\ne j\},\qquad \mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}=D_{\Lambda,N}/S_N,$$
where the permutation group $S_N$ acts by relabelling coordinates. Give $\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}$ the quotient sigma-algebra: $A\subseteq\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}$ is measurable exactly when its preimage under the quotient map $q_N:D_{\Lambda,N}\to\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}$ is measurable in the trace of the completed product-Lebesgue sigma-algebra. Identify each orbit with its unordered simple configuration. For $N=0$, set $\mathcal C_{\Lambda,0}=\{\varnothing\}$. If $\lambda_{\Lambda}^{\otimes N}$ is product Lebesgue measure restricted to $D_{\Lambda,N}$, define the sector reference measure by
$$\mu_{\Lambda,N}=\frac1{N!}(q_N)_\#\lambda_{\Lambda}^{\otimes N}\quad(N\geq1),\qquad \mu_{\Lambda,0}(\{\varnothing\})=1.$$
Equivalently, for every nonnegative measurable function $f$ on $\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}$,
$$\int f(\omega)\,\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega)=\frac1{N!}\int_{D_{\Lambda,N}}f(q_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N))\,d^{dN}x.$$
Collision diagonals have product Lebesgue measure zero, so $\mu_{\Lambda,N}(\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N})=|\Lambda|^N/N!$; in particular, symmetric integrands may use the equivalent integral over all of $\Lambda^N$. Thus $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ is a finite measure, not generally a probability. Two labelled tuples represent the same state exactly when they are in one $S_N$ orbit. The factor $1/N!$ is an adopted indistinguishable-particle positional convention, not a theorem about classical trajectories or every classical description.

Let $\mathcal C_\Lambda=\bigsqcup_{N\geq0}\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N}$ with the disjoint-union sigma-algebra, and regard each $\mu_{\Lambda,N}$ as a measure on this union supported on its $N$-point sector. Define the unit-intensity finite-region Poisson reference by
$$Q_\Lambda=e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N=0}^{\infty}\mu_{\Lambda,N}.$$
Its total mass is one because $\mu_{\Lambda,N}(\mathcal C_{\Lambda,N})=|\Lambda|^N/N!$ and $e^{-|\Lambda|}\sum_{N\geq0}|\Lambda|^N/N!=1$. This is a positional reference measure in the chosen dimensionless coordinates; it supplies no empirical claim about particle trajectories.

Use $\Lambda_n=[-n-\tfrac12,n+\tfrac12)^d$, its side length $L_n=2n+1$ and dimensionless volume $V_n=L_n^d$, the periodic positional energy $H_{L_n,\mathrm{per}}$ of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], and the exact-$N$ measure $\mu_{\Lambda_n,N}$ of [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. ## Definition

Let $u,v$ be finite-support real coefficient maps on the tagged state labels of [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]] with equal total coefficient. For a typed state $x$, compound notation uses the represented map $\mathsf{J}(x)$ from [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]; its raw unit point mass is $e_{(\Gamma,x)}$. Signed maps still use the ordinary total of their raw coefficients, exactly the bookkeeping mass of the represented nonnegative maps. Put $d=v-u$, $d^+(x)=\max(d(x),0)$ and $d^-(x)=\max(-d(x),0)$. Define $u\preceq_s v$ to mean $d^-\prec d^+$ under the compound relation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Write $u\sim_s v$ when both $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s u$. These are formal signed comparison maps, not physical negative amounts. The positive and negative parts are finite-support compounds of equal mass. If $u\sim_s v$, then $cu\sim_s cv$ for every real $c$: positive $c$ uses scaling, $c=0$ is reflexivity, and negative $c$ swaps the positive and negative parts while equivalence supplies both comparison directions. This Definition introduces the signed notation; ordinary-order compatibility and the signed-order laws are proved separately.

## Statement

Under A1–A6 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for compounds $A,B$ with $m(A)=m(B)$ and every finite spectator compound $C$, $A+C\prec B+C$ if and only if $A\prec B$. Consequently, for finite-support signed maps $u,v$ of equal total coefficient, define $u\preceq_s v$ by $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$. This relation is well-defined, agrees with $\prec$ on nonnegative maps, is invariant under adding a common signed map, is transitive, and is closed under addition of two comparisons. No comparison hypothesis is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Finite-support nonnegative compound maps, equal-mass comparisons, and A1–A6.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the compound relation is reflexive and transitive, composition-consistent, positively scale-invariant, admits splitting/recombination, and satisfies the stated fixed-spectator stability axiom. It does not assume CH.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-tagged-scalable-compound]]: compounds are finite-support nonnegative maps; their total coefficient masses add under composition and scale under nonnegative dilation. [[lem-tdmath-compound-mass-well-defined]] also proves that zero mass is equivalent to the empty map; the spectator need not have the same mass as either base.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: for equal-total finite-support maps $u,v$, $u\preceq_s v$ means $(v-u)^-\prec(v-u)^+$, with common signed translation leaving the difference unchanged.

[F3] [[def-canonical-natural]] and [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] give the canonical embedding $\iota_{\mathbb N}:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$, whose successor values are positive and are finite sums of $1$. [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]] gives the real sequence $\epsilon_k=1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(k))>0$, $k\in\mathbb N$, with $\epsilon_k\to0$.

## Proof

1.1 Suppose $A+C\prec B+C$ and $m(C)>0$. For each $k\in\mathbb N$, set $n=\sigma(k)$ and $r=\iota_{\mathbb N}(n)>0$, and write $A/r=(1/r)A$. The embedding's successor rule and finite induction show that the sum of $n$ copies of $A/r$ is $r(A/r)=A$, and likewise for $B$. Scaling the given comparison by $1/r$ gives $A/r+C/r\prec B/r+C/r$. By composition consistency, replace the $n$ copies of $A/r$ one at a time by $B/r$, keeping the already replaced copies, the remaining copies, and $C/r$ as spectators; after these finitely many replacements, $A+\epsilon_k C\prec B+\epsilon_k C$. This holds for every natural index $k$. By [F3], $\epsilon_k>0$ and $\epsilon_k\to0$, so stability with $Z_0=Z_1=C$ gives $A\prec B$. If $m(C)=0$, nonnegativity implies $C=0$ and the conclusion is the premise itself. Conversely, $A\prec B$ gives $A+C\prec B+C$ by consistency. [A1, F1, F3, algebra, induction]

2.1 For equal-total signed maps $u,v$, the difference $d=v-u$ has finite support and total coefficient zero, so $m(d^+)=m(d^-)$. If $u,v$ are nonnegative, their pointwise common part $k(x)=\min\{u(x),v(x)\}$ gives $u=k+d^-$ and $v=k+d^+$. Cancellation in step 1.1 proves $u\prec v$ exactly when $d^-\prec d^+$, which by [F2] is $u\preceq_s v$; adding a common signed map leaves $d$ unchanged by [F2]. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 If $u\preceq_s v$ and $v\preceq_s w$, [F2] identifies these with comparisons of $(v-u)^-$ to $(v-u)^+$ and $(w-v)^-$ to $(w-v)^+$. Consistency combines them. Their pointwise common minimum cancels by step 1.1, leaving $(w-u)^-\prec(w-u)^+$, which [F2] identifies as $u\preceq_s w$. The same finite-sum argument proves closure under addition; reflexivity follows from reflexivity of the zero compound. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the Euclidean norm $\|z\|=(\sum_{j=1}^d z_j^2)^{1/2}$, and balls $B(a,r)=\{z:\|z-a\|<r\}$. A set is open if it contains a ball about each of its points. Let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be finite and convex, meaning $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for every $x,y\in U$ and $t\in[0,1]$. For every $x_0\in U$, there are a neighborhood $V$ of $x_0$ and $L<\infty$ such that $|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|$ for all $x,y\in V$. The same conclusion holds for finite concave functions by applying the result to $-f$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The open convex domain, finite-valued function, and Euclidean norm.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: line segments and finite convex combinations of points in a convex set remain in that set.

## Proof

1.1 Choose a closed cube centered at $x_0$ whose concentric dilation by factor $2$ lies in $U$. Every point of the cube is a convex combination of its finitely many vertices, so [F1] and convexity bound $f$ above there by the largest vertex value $M$. If $x$ lies in the cube, then $2x_0-x$ lies in the dilated cube; convexity gives $f(x_0)\le(f(x)+f(2x_0-x))/2$, hence $f(x)\ge2f(x_0)-M'$, where $M'$ is the largest value of $f$ at the finitely many vertices of the dilated cube, an upper bound there by the same convex-combination argument. Thus $f$ is bounded above and below on a ball about $x_0$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Choose concentric balls $B(x_0,r)\subset B(x_0,2r)\subset U$ on which $m\le f\le M$. For distinct $x,y\in B(x_0,r/2)$, extend the segment from $x$ through $y$ to $z=y+(r/2)(y-x)/\|y-x\|$, which lies in $B(x_0,2r)$. Put $\theta=\|y-x\|/(r/2+\|y-x\|)$, so $y=(1-\theta)x+\theta z$. Convexity yields $f(y)-f(x)\le\theta(M-m)\le(2(M-m)/r)\|y-x\|$. Repeating with $x,y$ interchanged gives the reverse bound. Negation proves the concave case. [step 1.1, F1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For a nonempty set $C$, define $\operatorname{aff}C=\{\sum_{j=1}^N a_jc_j:N\ge1,\ c_j\in C,\ a_j\in\mathbb R,\ \sum_j a_j=1\}$. With a fixed $c_0\in C$, this is $c_0+\operatorname{span}\{c-c_0:c\in C\}$, where span consists of finite linear combinations. An affine Euclidean space is such a translate of a finite-dimensional linear subspace with its induced Euclidean distance. Relative balls use this distance; interior means containing a relative ball, and closure means every relative ball meets the set. Let $C$ be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$. Its relative interior $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is the interior in $H=\operatorname{aff}C$. Then $\operatorname{ri}_H C$ is nonempty. If $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$, $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, and $0\le t<1$, then $(1-t)w+ty\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonempty convex $C\subseteq H$ in finite dimension. Affine dimension is the dimension of its translation space.

[F1] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: every finite convex combination of points of $C$ belongs to $C$.

## Proof

1.1 Let $k=\dim(\operatorname{aff}C)$. If $k=0$, then $C$ is a singleton and is open in its affine hull. If $k>0$, the definition of affine hull supplies $k+1$ affinely independent points of $C$ spanning it. Their simplex lies in $C$ by [F1]. Its barycenter has all $k+1$ barycentric coordinates positive; sufficiently small coordinate perturbations preserve positivity and their sum one. Thus a relative neighborhood of that barycenter lies in the simplex, proving $\operatorname{ri}_H C\ne\varnothing$. [given, F1, construct]

2.1 Fix $w,y,t$ as in the Statement. The case $t=0$ is $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. Suppose $0<t<1$ and put $q=(1-t)w+ty$. Choose $r>0$ so the relative ball $B_H(w,r)$ lies in $C$. Since $y\in\overline{C}^{\,H}$, choose one $y_*\in C$ with $\|y_*-y\|<(1-t)r/(4t)$. For every $q'\in B_H(q,(1-t)r/4)$, put $w_*=(q'-ty_*)/(1-t)$. Then $\|w_*-w\|<r/2$, so $w_*\in C$ and $q'=(1-t)w_*+ty_*\in C$ by [F1]. A relative neighborhood of $q$ lies in $C$, so $q\in\operatorname{ri}_H C$. [given, F1, choose, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], for every simple state $x$, the forward sector $A_x=\{y\in\Gamma_i:x\prec y\}$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$. For collinear $y=tx+(1-t)z$, $0<t<1$, $y\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$, and $x\prec z$ implies $x\prec y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a nonempty open convex domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 include consistency, scaling, splitting, convex-combination access, and stability for positive spectators.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: a nonempty convex set has nonempty relative interior, and segments from a relative-interior point to a closure point, excluding the closure endpoint, remain in the relative interior.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: any finite common spectator cancels when the two bases have equal mass, under A1–A6 without CH.

## Proof

1.1 If $x\prec y$ and $x\prec z$, splitting gives $x\sim(tx,(1-t)x)$. Consistency, positive scaling, and transitivity then give $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(ty,(1-t)z)\prec ty+(1-t)z$, so the convex combination belongs to $A_x$. [A1, algebra]

1.2 Let $y=tx+(1-t)z$ with $0<t<1$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$. Splitting gives $y\sim(ty,(1-t)y)$. If $y\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $ty$ gives $(ty,(1-t)y)\prec(ty,(1-t)z)$. Compose and cancel the common $(1-t)z$ by [F2], then scale by $1/t$, to get $x\prec y$. If instead $x\prec z$, scaling by $1-t$ and adding $tx$ gives $(tx,(1-t)x)\prec(tx,(1-t)z)\prec y$; recombination gives $x\prec y$. [A1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Take $y\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. If $y\in A_x$, the claim is immediate. Otherwise choose $w\in\operatorname{ri} A_x$ by [F1]. Because $\Gamma_i$ is open, choose $z=w+(1+\eta)(y-w)\in\Gamma_i$ for some $\eta>0$. For every integer $n>1+\eta$, $y_n=(1+1/n)y-z/n=w+(1-\eta/n)(y-w)$ lies in $\operatorname{ri}A_x$ by [F1], so $x\prec y_n$. Also $y=\frac{n}{n+1}y_n+\frac1{n+1}z$. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] gives $(\frac n{n+1}y_n,\frac1{n+1}z)\prec y$; scaling by $(n+1)/n$ and using the reversible split of $y$ gives $(y_n,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Consistency adds the same spectator $z/n$ to $x\prec y_n$, and transitivity with step 2.1 gives $(x,z/n)\prec(y,y/n)$ for every $n>1+\eta$. Apply the stability hypothesis in [A1] to bases $x,y$, fixed positive equal-mass represented spectators $z,y$, and the tail sequence $\epsilon_m=1/(m+n_0)$ with $n_0>1+\eta$. It follows that $x\prec y$. Thus every relative closure point belongs to $A_x$. [A1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the Darboux integral on nondegenerate intervals and the convention $\int_a^a f=0$. Let $L\ge0$, $T>0$, and let $f:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous. If $f(t)\le L\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ for every $t\in[0,T]$, then $f(t)=0$ for every $t\in[0,T]$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A nonnegative continuous function and the stated integral inequality.

[F1] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

[F2] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-chain-rule]], and [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: the product rule, chain rule, and mean value theorem apply to the displayed differentiable real functions.

[F3] [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $(e^x)'=e^x$ for every real $x$.

[F4] [[def-darboux-integral]]: a Riemann/Darboux integrable real function is bounded.

## Proof

1.1 For a continuous function on $[a,b]$, the Darboux definition gives $m(b-a)\le\int_a^b f\le M(b-a)$ whenever $m\le f\le M$, because every lower and upper sum has these bounds. For $a<c<b$, concatenating partitions of $[a,c]$ and $[c,b]$ adds both their lower sums and their upper sums. By integrability [F1], choose on each interval a lower sum within $\eta$ of its integral and an upper sum within $\eta$ of its integral, and refine these finitely many partitions together. The concatenated sums sandwich $\int_a^b f$ within $2\eta$ of $\int_a^c f+\int_c^b f$; letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves additivity. This also holds when $c$ is an endpoint under the zero-interval convention. Define reversed integrals by $\int_b^a f=-\int_a^b f$. By [F1], the integral defining $h(t)=\int_0^t f(s)\,ds$ exists. Continuity of $f$ gives $h'(t)=f(t)$ on $(0,T)$: the difference quotient error is bounded by $\sup_{|s-t|\le|r|}|f(s)-f(t)|$, which tends to zero as $r\to0$. By [F4], choose a finite $M$ with $0\le f\le M$. Then $|h(t)-h(s)|=|\int_s^t f|\le M|t-s|$ for all $s,t\in[0,T]$, which proves continuity at the endpoints as well as in the interior. The hypothesis gives $h'\le Lh$, so [F2]–[F3] yield $g'(t)\le0$ for $g(t)=e^{-Lt}h(t)$ on $(0,T)$. The mean value theorem makes $g$ nonincreasing; since $g(0)=0$ and $g\ge0$, $g\equiv0$ and $h\equiv0$. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, algebra]

2.1 For any $t>0$, the nonnegative continuous function $f$ has integral $h(t)=0$. If $f(t_0)>0$ at any $t_0>0$, continuity gives a positive lower bound on a nonempty subinterval of $[0,t_0]$, contradicting $h(t_0)=0$. At $t=0$ the assumed inequality gives $f(0)\le0$; nonnegativity gives $f(0)=0$. Hence $f\equiv0$. [step 1.1, given] ∎

## Statement

For nonempty $C$, define $\operatorname{aff}C=\{\sum_{j=1}^N a_jc_j:N\ge1,\ c_j\in C,\ a_j\in\mathbb R,\ \sum_j a_j=1\}$. An affine Euclidean space is a translate of a finite-dimensional real linear subspace with the induced Euclidean metric. A supporting hyperplane at $z$ is $\{q:n\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ for a nonzero vector $n$, with $z$ in the set and all its points in one closed half-space. Let $C$ be a nonempty convex set in a finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space $H$ of dimension $k\ge1$, let $\operatorname{aff}C=H$, and put $K=\overline{C}^{\,H}$. If $z\in\partial_H K$ (that is, $z\in K$ and every relative neighborhood of $z$ meets $H\setminus K$), then there is a nonzero linear functional $\ell$ on the translation space of $H$ such that $\ell(q-z)\le0$ for all $q\in C$. If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine dimension at most $d-2$, then every $z\in C$ has at least two distinct ambient supporting hyperplanes containing $\operatorname{aff}C$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated finite-dimensional affine Euclidean space and convex set.

[F2] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F3] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean coordinates identify linear functionals with vectors and give the usual unit sphere.

[F4] [[thm-extreme-value-metric]]: a continuous real function on a nonempty compact metric space attains its minimum.

[F5] [[lem-finite-dimensional-unit-spheres-are-sequentially-compact]]: unit spheres in finite-dimensional normed spaces are sequentially compact without a choice principle.

[F6] [[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]: rational coordinates are dense in real coordinates.

[F7] [[lem-tdmath-reciprocal-naturals-tend-zero]] supplies the positive real sequence $\epsilon_m=1/\iota_{\mathbb N}(\sigma(m))$, $m\in\mathbb N$, decreasing to zero with the canonical-natural field convention.

## Proof

1.1 Fix affine coordinates $H\cong\mathbb R^k$. Closure preserves convexity without choosing approximating sequences: for $x,y\in K$ and any $\epsilon>0$, choose two points of $C$ within $\epsilon$ of them; their convex combination approximates $(1-t)x+ty$ within $\epsilon$, so this point lies in $K$. Enumerate rational $k$-tuples canonically by increasing sums of absolute numerators and positive denominators, breaking the finite ties lexicographically. Density [F6] and the open complement of $K$ show that for each $m\in\mathbb N$ at least one enumerated point lies in $B(z,\epsilon_m)\setminus K$. Let $z_m$ be the first such point. This is a uniquely specified sequence with $z_m\to z$, not a countable selection of arbitrary witnesses. [given, F3, F6, F7, construct]

2.1 The nonempty compact set $K\cap\overline B(z_m,\|z_m-z\|+1)$ contains $z$. By [F2] and [F4], squared distance to $z_m$ attains a minimum there, and every point outside that ball is farther than the candidate $z$. Thus a nearest point $q_m\in K$ exists. It is unique: if two distinct minimizers had squared distance $d_m^2$, their midpoint would have squared distance $d_m^2-\|q_m-q'_m\|^2/4$, contradicting minimality and convexity. Consequently $(q_m)$ is also canonically determined. Since $z_m\notin K$, put $u_m=(z_m-q_m)/\|z_m-q_m\|$. Expanding the distance at $q_m+t(q-q_m)$ and letting $t\downarrow0$ gives $u_m\cdot(q-q_m)\le0$ for every $q\in K$. Also $\|q_m-z\|\le2\|z_m-z\|\to0$. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Every $u_m$ has norm one. The exact choice-free sequential-compactness supplier [F5] gives a subsequence converging to a unit vector $u$. This introduces no additional choice hypothesis. [F3, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For every $q\in K$, pass to the limit in $u_m\cdot(q-q_m)\le0$ along that subsequence. Continuity of the Euclidean pairing and $q_m\to z$ give $u\cdot(q-z)\le0$. The unit vector $u$ defines a nonzero supporting functional for $K$, hence for $C$, at $z$. [F3, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 If $C\subset\mathbb R^d$ has affine hull $H$ of dimension at most $d-2$, write its direction space as the span of $k\le d-2$ independent vectors $b_1,\ldots,b_k$. Its orthogonal complement is the solution space of the $k$ homogeneous equations $b_j\cdot n=0$. Row reduction has at most $k$ pivot variables, leaving at least $d-k\ge2$ free variables. Assigning one free variable the value one and the others zero gives two independent solutions (their free-coordinate vectors are different unit vectors). Thus choose two nonparallel nonzero normals $n_1,n_2$ orthogonal to the direction space of $H$. For each $j$, the hyperplane $\{q:n_j\cdot(q-z)=0\}$ contains $H$ and therefore supports $C$ at $z$. The two hyperplanes are distinct because their normals are not parallel. [given, F3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], every forward sector $A_x$ has nonempty interior in its ambient simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex $\Gamma_i\subset\mathbb R^d$, $d=n_i+1$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each sector is supported at every state by exactly one hyperplane, and every state has a strict successor.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$; if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$ by transitivity.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at its relative boundary in its affine hull, and a set of affine dimension at most $d-2$ has at least two distinct ambient supports through each of its points.

Thus take $d\ge2$. The affine hull of $A_x$ has dimension at most $d-1$. If its dimension were at most $d-2$, [F2] would give two distinct supporting hyperplanes at $x$, contradicting S2. Hence its affine hull is a hyperplane $H$; this $H$ supports $A_x$ at every point, including $x$. [A1, F2]

1.2 By S1 choose $y$ with $x\prec\prec y$. Then $y\in A_x$ and $x\notin A_y$. Transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x\subseteq H$. If $A_y$ had affine dimension at most $d-2$, [F2] would again give multiple ambient supports at $y$, contrary to S2. Thus $\operatorname{aff}A_y=H$. [A1, F1, F2]

1.3 Choose $w\in\operatorname{ri}_H A_y$ by [F3]. The segment from $w$ to $x$ is contained in $H\cap\Gamma_i$ by convexity of both sets, starts in $A_y$, and ends outside $A_y$. Its intersection with $A_y$ is closed by relative closedness [F1], so it has a last point $z$ before $x$. Points immediately after $z$ on this segment lie outside $A_y$ and, because $A_y$ is closed in the open set $\Gamma_i$, outside $\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. Thus $z\in\partial_H\overline{A_y}^{\,H}$. The support statement [F2] supplies a nonzero functional on $H$ whose zero hyperplane supports $A_y$ at $z$. [F1, F2, F3, choose]

2.1 Extend this functional to the ambient Euclidean space by taking its normal vector in the direction space of $H$. Its zero hyperplane contains the within-$H$ support and is not $H$ itself. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y$, so the extended plane supports $A_z$ at $z$; the plane $H$ also supports $A_z$. These are distinct, contradicting S2 at $z$. Therefore $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior. [A1, F1, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Use the Euclidean distance $\|q-z\|$; $\operatorname{int}K$ consists of points containing a ball in $K$, closure consists of points whose every ball meets $K$, and $\partial K=\overline K\setminus\operatorname{int}K$. Closed means equal to closure. A supporting hyperplane at $x\in K$ is $\{q:n\cdot(q-x)=0\}$ with $n\ne0$ and $K$ contained in one closed half-space. Let $K\subset\mathbb R^d$ be closed and convex with nonempty interior, $d\ge1$, and let $x\in\partial K$. Suppose $K$ has exactly one supporting hyperplane at $x$. Choose its inward unit normal $n$, so $n\cdot(q-x)\ge0$ for every $q\in K$. Then for every $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$, there is $\delta>0$ such that $x+tv\in\operatorname{int}K$ for every $0<t<\delta$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The closed convex set, boundary point, unique supporting hyperplane, and Euclidean inner product.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-closed-convex-separation]]: a point outside a nonempty closed convex Euclidean set admits a strict separating linear functional.

[F2] [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: Euclidean linear functionals are represented by vectors.

[F4] [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]: finite convex combinations of points in a convex set remain in it.



## Proof

1.1 Let $T=\overline{\{a(q-x):a\ge0,\ q\in K\}}$. This is a closed convex cone. If a nonzero functional $\ell$ is nonnegative on $T$, then it is nonnegative on $K-x$, so its zero plane through $x$ supports $K$. Uniqueness in the hypothesis makes that plane the plane with normal $n$; the inward sign forces $\ell=c n\cdot(\,\cdot\,)$ for some $c>0$. [given, F2]

2.1 The support at $x$ gives $T\subseteq\{w:n\cdot w\ge0\}$. If $v$ with $n\cdot v>0$ were outside $T$, strict separation [F1] of $v$ from the cone would give a nonzero functional $\ell$ nonnegative on $T$ and negative at $v$: the separating bound is zero because $0\in T$ and $T$ is a cone. Step 1.1 then makes $\ell$ a positive multiple of $n$, contradicting $n\cdot v>0$. Thus the open half-space $n\cdot w>0$ lies in $T$, and each such $v$ is an interior point of $T$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Fix such $v$. Since $v\in\operatorname{int}T$, choose $d+1$ affinely independent vectors in a small ball about $v$ whose simplex contains a neighborhood of $v$. 4.1 Choose $\delta>0$ with $\delta A<1$. ## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], each simple domain has one orientation sign $\varepsilon_i\in\{-1,1\}$, constant across the domain, such that at fixed work coordinate $v$, $x\prec y$ exactly when $\varepsilon_i(u_y-u_x)\ge0$. In coordinates oriented so $\varepsilon_i=1$, for each $x\in\Gamma_i$ the projection $\rho_x$ of $\partial_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ onto work coordinates is open and connected; the boundary is the graph $(u_x(v),v)$ of a $C^1$ function with locally Lipschitz derivative

$$Du_x(v)=-P_i(u_x(v),v).$$

If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y=A_x$ and their boundary graphs agree.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on an open convex simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: each $A_x$ is supported at $x$ by a unique finite-slope plane; $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: $A_x$ is convex and closed relative to $\Gamma_i$, and its collinear order implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every $A_x$ has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-relative-boundary-support]]: a convex set has a support at each relative boundary point of its closure in its affine hull.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-unique-support-inward-ray]]: at a full-dimensional convex set's boundary point with a unique support, every direction strictly toward the supporting half-space's interior enters the set's interior for all sufficiently small positive steps.

[F5] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: every finite convex function on an open convex set is locally Lipschitz.

[F6] [[lem-tdmath-integral-zero-uniqueness]]: a nonnegative continuous function bounded by a constant times its zero-start integral is identically zero.

[F7] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F8] [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], and [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]: the stated $C^1$ maps have total derivatives, and the derivative of a composition of Euclidean maps is the composition of those derivatives.

[F9] [[thm-newton-leibniz-with-interior-derivative]]: a continuous function on a closed interval, differentiable in its interior with an integrable derivative extension, has endpoint increment equal to the integral of that derivative.

[F10] [[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]: a continuous real function on a compact interval is Riemann integrable.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1] and [F1]–[F10]. Write a support plane's inward unit normal with energy component nonzero, as ensured by its finite-slope form.

1.1 To apply [F4] to a sector at a boundary point $z$, choose $r>0$ with $\overline B(z,r)\subset\Gamma_i$ and put $K=A_x\cap\overline B(z,r)$. This is globally closed and convex, and agrees with $A_x$ near $z$. It has nonempty interior: join $z$ to an interior point of $A_x$ and take points sufficiently close to $z$. Supporting planes at $z$ coincide for $K$ and $A_x$: a local supporting inequality extends along every segment from $z$ to a point of $A_x$. Any such plane also supports $A_z\subseteq A_x$ at $z$, so S2 makes it unique. Thus [F4] applies to $K$ and its interior conclusions hold for $A_x$ locally. For fixed $x=(u_x,v_x)$, the vertical section $I_x:=\{u:(u,v_x)\in A_x\}$ is a relatively closed convex interval by [F1]. The support plane at $x$ confines it to one side of $u_x$. Its inward normal has nonzero energy component, so [F4] gives a nontrivial interior vertical segment on that side. [A1, F1, F2, F4]


1.2 Let $u,w$ be two $C^1$ graph solutions of $Dq=-P_i(q,v)$ on a common open domain, and suppose $u(v_0)=w(v_0)$. Since $P_i$ is locally Lipschitz, choose a convex neighborhood of $(u(v_0),v_0)$ on which one Lipschitz constant $L$ works. Continuity of $u,w$ lets us choose a convex ball about $v_0$ whose closure lies in the common domain and whose two graph images stay in that neighborhood; take any $v$ in a smaller concentric ball. Put $d=v-v_0$ and $\gamma(t)=v_0+td$ for $0\le t\le1$. By [F8], $r(t)=u(\gamma(t))-w(\gamma(t))$ is $C^1$ and
$r'(t)=[-P_i(u(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))+P_i(w(\gamma(t)),\gamma(t))]\cdot d.$
The local Lipschitz bound for $P_i$ gives $|r'(t)|\le L\|d\||r(t)|$. The derivative is continuous, hence integrable by [F10]; [F9] gives $r(t)=\int_0^t r'(s)\,ds$; hence $h(t):=|r(t)|\le L\|d\|\int_0^t h(s)\,ds$. Apply [F6] on $[0,1]$ to obtain $h=0$. Thus $u=w$ near $v_0$. Along any polygonal path in the common open domain, the set of path parameters at which equality holds is closed by continuity and open by this local result; since the path interval is connected and the set is nonempty, equality holds along the whole path. Every open connected subset of Euclidean space is polygonally connected: points reachable from a fixed point by finitely many segments in small balls form a nonempty relatively open and relatively closed set. Therefore equality extends throughout each common connected domain. [A1, F6, F8, F9, F10, given, construct]

2.1 The convex, relatively closed interval $I_x$ contains a nontrivial segment on the inward side by step 1.1 and [F4]. Suppose it does not contain the whole open $\Gamma_i$-fiber on that side. Let $x_1$ be its midpoint. Since $x_1\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_{x_1}\subseteq A_x$. The supporting plane of $A_{x_1}$ has nonzero energy coefficient, so its vertical section lies wholly on one side of $x_1$; being contained in $I_x$, it lies in one half of $[x,b]$ and has at most half its length. It is nonempty and closed relative to $[x,b]$, hence compact. Repeat: take the midpoint $x_{k+1}$ of the current compact interval $I_{x_k}$; then $x_k\prec x_{k+1}$, so the next section is nested inside the current one and again has at most half its length. These intervals have nonempty total intersection: otherwise their open complements would cover the first compact interval, a finite subcover would do so by [F7], and nesting would make one interval empty. Their lengths tend to zero, so the intersection has a unique point $x_\infty$, still in the first interval contained in $\Gamma_i$. The midpoint recursion and this unique intersection require no selection from an arbitrary countable family. Relative closedness puts $x_\infty$ in every $A_{x_k}$, hence $A_{x_\infty}\subseteq A_{x_k}$ by transitivity. Its vertical section is therefore only $\{x_\infty\}$, contradicting the nontrivial interior vertical segment at $x_\infty$ supplied by [F4]. Thus $I_x$ contains the whole open fiber on its inward side. [A1, F1, F4, F7, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 All states on a fixed work-coordinate fiber have the same orientation. If $x$ is oriented upward and a state $z$ above it were oriented downward, the full upward section from step 2.1 gives $x\prec z$, and the full downward section from $z$ gives $z\prec w$ for a state $w$ below $x$, contradicting the support at $x$. If a state $y$ below an upward $x$ were oriented downward, choose $z$ above $x$ with $x\prec z$; the first collinear implication in [F1], applied to $x$ between $y$ and $z$, gives $y\prec x$, contradicting the downward support at $y$. The reversed argument handles a downward $x$. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 By step 3.1, orientation is constant on each fixed-work fiber. The fiber orientation is locally constant in $v$. At any $x$, choose one vertical point just inside the supported half-space and one just outside; by [F4] the inside point can be chosen in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. Openness of $\Gamma_i$ and of the interior and exterior regions preserves these memberships on nearby fibers. Each such fiber therefore meets $\partial A_x$ between these two energy values. A support of $A_x$ at that boundary point also supports the point's own sector and so has its S2 orientation; the inside/outside placement fixes that orientation. Thus nearby fibers have the same sign as the fiber through $x$. Since $\Gamma_i$ is convex, it is connected; a locally constant two-valued sign is constant. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Adopt the coordinate convention $\varepsilon_i=1$. Step 2.1 and the common orientation give $x\prec y$ exactly for $u_y\ge u_x$ at fixed $v$, with strict comparison for $u_y>u_x$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Put $\rho_x=\pi_v(\partial A_x)$. At a boundary point $z\in\partial A_x$, [F3] supplies a support to $A_x$. Because $A_z\subseteq A_x$, that plane also supports $A_z$ and equals its unique S2 plane. Its finite slope gives a nonvertical inward direction; [F4] supplies nearby vertical points inside $A_x$, while the opposite side is outside by the support. Neighborhoods of one inside and one outside point show every nearby work fiber meets $\partial A_x$. Hence $\rho_x$ is open. It is connected because S3 makes $\partial A_x$ arcwise connected and projection is continuous. By step 5.1, every vertical fiber over $\rho_x$ has exactly one boundary energy; call it $u_x(v)$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 5.1]

7.1 For $v,v'\in\rho_x$, convexity of $A_x$ puts every convex combination of their boundary states in $A_x$. On any sufficiently small convex ball in $\rho_x$, the unique-boundary property and upward orientation make $u_x$ the least energy in each fiber. Therefore $u_x(tv+(1-t)v')\le t u_x(v)+(1-t)u_x(v')$, so $u_x$ is finite and convex there. It is locally Lipschitz by [F5]. The inward support at $(u_x(v),v)$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\ge -P_i(u_x(v),v)\cdot(v'-v).$
The support at $(u_x(v'),v')$ gives
$u_x(v')-u_x(v)\le -P_i(u_x(v'),v')\cdot(v'-v).$

8.1 If $y\in\partial A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$. The boundary graphs agree at $v_y$ and solve the same differential equation. The set of $v\in\rho_y$ where $v\in\rho_x$ and $u_y(v)=u_x(v)$ is nonempty, open by step 1.2, and closed by continuity and relative closedness of $\partial A_x$. Connectedness of $\rho_y$ makes it all of $\rho_y$. This shows $\rho_y\subseteq\rho_x$. The same argument, using relative closedness of $\partial A_y$, shows $\rho_y$ is relatively closed in connected $\rho_x$; it is relatively open because both projections are open. Hence $\rho_x=\rho_y$ and the boundary graphs agree. In particular $x\in\partial A_y$, so $y\prec x$; together with $y\in A_x$ and transitivity this gives $A_x=A_y$. [A1, F1, step 7.1, step 1.2] ∎

## Statement

Let a family of simple domains satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and suppose every pair has an admitted simple thermal join satisfying T1 and T2 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then the fixed-work orientation signs from [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]] agree throughout the family. One common affine proof-coordinate convention $u'=\varepsilon u$, $\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}$, therefore makes each fixed-work accessibility order increase with $u'$ and preserves the energy-sum formula for joins. This is a mathematical coordinate convention; it does not change a physical energy quantity or assert a sign of a measured temperature.

## Facts & Assumptions

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: the component charts are open, represented states have their positive type weights, and the relation is composition-consistent and transitive.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1 sends every admissible split to its join; T2 supplies, for each join state, at least one admissible split accessible in both directions to that join state, at the same summed energy and work coordinates.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each component domain has a constant sign $\varepsilon_\Gamma$ with fixed-work comparison equivalent to $\varepsilon_\Gamma(u_y-u_x)\ge0$.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: any finite common spectator cancels when the two bases have equal mass; its mass need not equal the base mass.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [A2], [F1], and [F2].

1.1 Suppose two component signs are opposed. Choose a join state $Z$ and a reversible split $(x,y)$ by T2 in [A2]. Write $x=(u_x,v_x)$ and $y=(u_y,v_y)$. Openness in [A1] permits a sufficiently small nonzero $\delta$ with $x'=(u_x+\delta,v_x)$ and $y'=(u_y-\delta,v_y)$ in their respective charts. Choose the sign of $\delta$ so $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_x}\delta>0$; opposed signs imply $\varepsilon_{\Gamma_y}(-\delta)>0$. Thus [F1] gives $x\prec\prec x'$ and $y\prec\prec y'$. These pairs have the same summed energy and work coordinates and the same represented aggregate composition and mass. [A1, A2, F1, construct]

2.1 If $(x',y')\prec(x,y)$, consistency with $y\prec y'$ gives $(x',y)\prec(x',y')\prec(x,y)$. Cancel the common represented spectator $y$ by [F2] to get $x'\prec x$, contrary to step 1.1. But T1 gives $(x',y')\prec Z$, and the chosen T2 split gives $Z\prec(x,y)$, so transitivity produces exactly this forbidden reverse comparison. Opposed signs are impossible. Every pair has an admitted join, hence one common sign $\varepsilon$ works for the whole family. The affine change $u'=\varepsilon u$ preserves openness and convexity and sends $u=u_x+u_y$ to $u'=\varepsilon u_x+\varepsilon u_y$; its positive orientation describes the same accessibility relation. No physical energy, unit or calibration premise is redefined. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

## Statement

Under T1–T3 and the equal-state reversible split in [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]], if $x\sim_T y$ then $s x\sim_T t y$ for every $s,t>0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The contact and scaling assumptions for tagged states and their joins.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: each equal-state scaled pair is reversibly equivalent to its join, and thermal equivalence is transitive.

## Proof

1.1 Let $x$ be any typed state and $s>0$. ## Statement

Under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], the sectors are nested: if $y\in A_x$, then $A_y\subseteq A_x$; equality holds when $y\in\partial A_x$, and $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$ when $y\in\operatorname{int}_{\Gamma_i}A_x$.
