## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A7 and S1–S3 on a simple domain $\Gamma_i$.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: $A_x$ is defined by $x\prec y$, every state is in its own sector, and each support plane is unique.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-convex-sector-closedness]]: sectors are convex and relatively closed; the collinear implications hold.

[F2] [[lem-tdmath-sector-interior]]: every sector has nonempty ambient interior.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: if $w\in\partial A_x$, then $A_w=A_x$.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-relative-interior-segment]]: if $w$ is in the relative interior of a convex set and $q$ lies in its closure, then $(1-t)w+tq$ lies in the relative interior for every $0\le t<1$.

## Proof

1.1 If $y\in A_x$, transitivity gives $A_y\subseteq A_x$. If also $y\in\partial A_x$, [F3] gives equality. Suppose instead $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. If $A_y$ met $\partial A_x$ at $z$, then $z\in A_y$ and [F3] would give $A_z=A_x$. Since $z\in A_y$, transitivity gives $A_z\subseteq A_y\subseteq A_x$, so $A_y=A_x$. But S2 puts $y$ on $\partial A_y$, contradicting $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. Thus $A_y$ avoids $\partial A_x$ and, being a subset of the closed sector $A_x$, lies in $\operatorname{int}A_x$. [A1, F3, algebra]

1.2 Suppose neither $y\in A_x$ nor $x\in A_y$. Choose $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ using [F2]. The segment from $y$ to $z$ lies in $\Gamma_i$ and meets $\partial A_x$ at a point $w$ strictly between its endpoints. By [F3], $A_w=A_x$, so $w\prec z$. The collinear implication in [F1], applied to $w=ty+(1-t)z$, gives $y\prec w\prec z$. Hence every $z\in\operatorname{int}A_x$ lies in $A_y$. Reversing $x,y$ gives $\operatorname{int}A_y\subseteq A_x$. [A1, F1, F2, F3]

2.1 Because $A_x$ is full-dimensional by [F2], its affine hull is the ambient space. Fix $w\in\operatorname{int}A_x$. For any $q\in A_x$, relative closedness gives $q\in\overline{A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$, and [F4] puts $(1-t)w+tq$ in $\operatorname{int}A_x$ for every $0\le t<1$. Letting $t\uparrow1$ shows $q\in\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$. The reverse inclusion follows because $A_x$ is relatively closed. Hence $A_x=\overline{\operatorname{int}A_x}^{\,\Gamma_i}$; the same holds for $A_y$. Relative closedness from [F1] therefore extends the two interior inclusions in step 1.2 to $A_x\subseteq A_y$ and $A_y\subseteq A_x$. Equality would put $x\in A_y$, contradicting the supposition. Thus at least one of $x\prec y$ or $y\prec x$ always holds. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

3.1 If $x\prec y$, then $y\in A_x$. If $y$ is a boundary point, step 1.1 gives $A_x=A_y$, hence $x\prec y$ and $y\prec x$. Otherwise step 1.1 gives $A_y\subset\operatorname{int}A_x$, and $x\notin A_y$ because S2 places $x$ on $\partial A_x$. Thus $x\prec\prec y$. Conversely, if $y\in\operatorname{int}A_x$, step 1.1 and S2 show $x\notin A_y$, so $x\prec\prec y$. [A1, F1, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let a simple domain and its finite thermal joins satisfy [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Let $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$, and let $x$ satisfy $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$. For $0\le\lambda\le1$, write $R_\lambda$ for the compound state $((1-\lambda)x_0,\lambda x_1)$, omitting a zero coefficient at the endpoints. Then there is a unique $\lambda\in(0,1)$ with $R_\lambda\sim x$ in the common accessibility relation.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The compound axioms A1–A6, thermal-join axioms T1–T3 with the equal-state split, strict strip endpoints, and join closure.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: compounds have the preorder, consistency, positive scaling, splitting, and stability assumptions; CH is not part of this definition.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] and [[lem-tdmath-thermal-scaling-invariance]]: an equal-state split is reversible, thermal equivalence is transitive, and scaling either member of a thermal-equilibrium pair preserves thermal equivalence.

[F2] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: equal-total signed maps compare by their positive and negative parts; cancellation is valid under A1–A6 without CH.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: every pair of states in each finite join domain is comparable.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3], and $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$.

1.1 For $0\le\lambda<\mu\le1$, the signed difference $R_\mu-R_\lambda=(\mu-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$ has positive part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and negative part $(\mu-\lambda)\mathsf{J}(x_0)$. Since $x_0\prec x_1$, positive scaling and [F2] give $R_\lambda\prec R_\mu$. A reverse comparison would, by [F2] and inverse positive scaling, give $x_1\prec x_0$, contrary to strictness. Thus the reference states are strictly ordered by parameter. [A1, F2, algebra]

1.2 For $0<\lambda<1$, [F1] makes $(1-\lambda)x_0$ and $\lambda x_1$ thermally equivalent. By the definition of thermal equivalence, their compound is reversible with its join state. The equal-state split makes $((1-\lambda)x,\lambda x)$ reversible with its join state and with $x$. Both join states belong to the join of two scaled copies of the same simple domain, so [F3] compares them. The endpoint cases use $R_0=x_0$ and $R_1=x_1$ directly. Hence $R_\lambda$ and $x$ are comparable for every $\lambda\in[0,1]$. [F1, F3, given]

2.1 Let $L=\{\lambda\in[0,1]:R_\lambda\prec x\}$. The strict endpoint comparison $x_0\prec x$ puts $0$ in $L$. Step 1.1 and transitivity make $L$ downward closed. Let $s=\sup L$. If $s>0$, then $s-1/n\in L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Since $R_{s-1/n}+(1/n)x_1=R_s+(1/n)x_0$, consistency yields $R_s+(1/n)x_0\prec x+(1/n)x_1$. Stability with bases $R_s,x$ and fixed spectators $x_0,x_1$ gives $R_s\prec x$. If $s=0$, this comparison is the given $x_0\prec x$. [A1, F2, step 1.1, choose]

3.1 If $s<1$, then $s+1/n\notin L$ for every sufficiently large $n$. Step 1.2 gives comparability and the definition of $L$ excludes $R_{s+1/n}\prec x$, so $x\prec R_{s+1/n}$. The identity $R_{s+1/n}+(1/n)x_0=R_s+(1/n)x_1$ and stability yield $x\prec R_s$. If $s=1$, the strict strip gives $x\prec R_1$; together with step 2.1 this would imply $x_1\prec x$, contrary to $x\prec\prec x_1$. Thus $s<1$, and step 2.1 and the preceding stability comparison give $R_s\sim x$. [A1, F2, step 1.2, step 2.1]

4.1 The equivalence $R_s\sim x$ also excludes $s=0$, because $R_0=x_0$ and $x_0\not\sim x$, and excludes $s=1$ by strictness of $x\prec\prec x_1$. If $R_t\sim x$ for another $t$, transitivity gives $R_s\sim R_t$; step 1.1 then forces $s=t$. Hence the parameter is unique and lies in $(0,1)$. [F2, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and T1–T4 of [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]] for every finite join. For any one simple type $\Gamma_i$, every two finite compounds of its scaled copies with the same total coefficient mass are comparable. Thus CH holds on all multiple scaled products of that type. No entropy across different material types is asserted here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The stated forward-sector and thermal-contact hypotheses; every thermal join remains a simple domain with these hypotheses.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7, S1–S3, and the tagged finite-compound conventions hold, without an assumed CH.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T4 provide simple thermal joins, reversible equilibrium splits, thermal scaling, and a thermal endpoint pair surrounding each state.

[F1] [[lem-tdmath-reference-strip-coordinate]]: every state in a strip with strict thermally equivalent endpoints is equivalent to a unique reference mixture with parameter in $(0,1)$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: one-copy comparisons hold on each finite join domain; strict comparison is interior membership, and forward sectors are nested.

[F3] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparison is defined from positive/negative parts; it is translation invariant, additive, and cancellable under A1–A6.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each simple domain has one constant fixed-work energy orientation; arbitrarily close states on a vertical segment are strictly ordered in that orientation.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: a closed bounded subset of finite-dimensional Euclidean space is compact.

## Proof

1.1 By T4, the open strips $\Sigma(a,b):=\{x:a\prec\prec x\prec\prec b\}$ with $a\prec\prec b$ and $a\sim_T b$ cover $\Gamma_i$. They are open: by [F2], $a\prec\prec x$ is $x\in\operatorname{int}A_a$, and $x\prec\prec b$ is $x\notin A_b$; the latter set is open because $A_b$ is relatively closed. [A1, A2, F2]

1.2 Let $\Sigma(a,b)$ and $\Sigma(c,d)$ overlap. Their intersection is open. Choose two states $e\prec\prec f$ in a small vertical segment contained in the overlap, using [F4]. Let $s_e,s_f$ be their coordinates in the first strip and $t_e,t_f$ in the second, supplied by [F1]. If $s_f<s_e$, the signed difference $R_{s_e}-R_{s_f}=(s_e-s_f)(\mathsf{J}(b)-\mathsf{J}(a))$ and positive scaling and signed compatibility [A1, F3] give $R_{s_f}\prec R_{s_e}$, so $f\prec e$ by the two reference equivalences; if $s_f=s_e$, those references coincide and give $f\sim e$. Both contradict $e\prec\prec f$. Hence $s_f>s_e$, and the same argument gives $t_f>t_e$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, construct]

2.1 The four reference equivalences give, in signed comparison,
$f-e\sim_s(s_f-s_e)(b-a),\qquad f-e\sim_s(t_f-t_e)(d-c).$
Put $r=(s_f-s_e)/(t_f-t_e)>0$. Additivity and positive scaling in [F3] give $d-c\sim_s r(b-a)$. Applying the same algebra to the equivalences for $e$ gives $c\sim_s a+(s_e-r t_e)(b-a)$. Consequently a state in the second strip with coordinate $t$ has first-chart coordinate $s_e+r(t-t_e)$. The change of chart is affine with strictly positive slope. [F1, F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The same calculation covers a finite chain of overlapping strips: after each overlap, express the new strip's endpoint states as signed-equivalent affine maps in the existing reference pair. The local strip lemma gives every state $z$ of the added strip a coordinate $s_z\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ in the existing chart. Signed addition, positive scaling, translation, and equivalence under negative scaling are valid by [F3]; hence induction along a finite overlap chain gives one such common chart for every state in the union. [F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Take any finite list of target states in $\Gamma_i$ and join them in order by finitely many straight segments, which lie in $\Gamma_i$ by convexity. The resulting connected path is a finite union of closed bounded segments, hence compact by [F5]. The open strips from step 1.1 cover it, so compactness gives a finite subcover. The intersection graph of those strips meeting the path is connected: otherwise their unions would partition the connected path into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Order a spanning tree from one root strip; each later strip overlaps an earlier one in an open set and can be glued by step 3.1. Thus every target state has a common signed chart $\mathsf{J}(z)\sim_s(1-s_z)\mathsf{J}(a)+s_z\mathsf{J}(b)$ with $a\prec\prec b$. [A1, F5, step 1.1, step 3.1, construct]

5.1 Write the arbitrary scaled-copy compounds as
$$A=\sum_j\alpha_j\mathsf{J}_{r_j\Gamma_i}(r_jx_j),\qquad B=\sum_k\beta_k\mathsf{J}_{h_k\Gamma_i}(h_ky_k),$$
with $r_j,h_k>0$ and nonnegative coefficients, omitting zero terms. The declared reversible transport in [A1] gives $\mathsf{J}_{r_j\Gamma_i}(r_jx_j)\sim r_j\mathsf{J}_{\Gamma_i}(x_j)$ and similarly on the other side; ordinary positive scaling and composition therefore reduce them to the unscaled base-type states with effective amounts $a_j=\alpha_jr_j$ and $b_k=\beta_kh_k$. Their masses are respectively $r_jw_{\Gamma_i}$ and $h_kw_{\Gamma_i}$ before this transport, so equal total mass $M$ implies
$$L=M/w_{\Gamma_i}=\sum_j a_j=\sum_k b_k.$$
If $M=0$, both maps are empty and reflexivity applies. Otherwise use step 4.1 for the finite list of base states $x_j,y_k$, with common-chart coordinates $s_j,t_k$. Signed addition and splitting [F3] make the transported compounds equivalent to $R_{q_A}=(L-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_A\mathsf{J}(b)$ and $R_{q_B}=(L-q_B)\mathsf{J}(a)+q_B\mathsf{J}(b)$, where $q_A=\sum_j a_js_j$ and $q_B=\sum_k b_kt_k$. If $q_A<q_B$, their signed difference has positive part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(b)$ and negative part $(q_B-q_A)\mathsf{J}(a)$, so $a\prec b$ and positive scaling compare them; equality gives reflexivity, and $q_B<q_A$ gives the reverse comparison. Transitivity transfers this order through the reversible transports to the original distinct scaled tags. Hence CH holds for every allowed scaled-copy pair, without identifying those tags or dropping their scale factors. [A1, F3, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$ be a simple domain satisfying the forward-sector hypotheses and T1–T4. Let $S$ be the additive extensive entropy supplied by [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]] after CH for its finite scaled products is proved by [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]. Then either all pairs of states in $\Gamma$ are thermally equivalent, or there are $x,y$ on one entropy level (equivalently, one adiabat $\partial A_x$ by [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]) with $x\not\sim_T y$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The same-type accessibility relation, the thermal relation, the hypotheses in the Statement, and the current entropy representation.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 and S1–S3 hold; the sector theorem supplies a constant fixed-work energy orientation for each type.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T4 hold and thermal equivalence is transitive.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]: every equal-mass finite compound comparison of this simple type is complete.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: under that comparison property, an additive extensive entropy represents every same-type finite-compound comparison.

[F3] [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: each simple domain has a constant orientation sign for fixed-work energy comparisons; in coordinates oriented in that sign, sector boundaries are the stated graphs.

[F4] [[lem-tdmath-convex-function-local-lipschitz]]: a finite concave entropy is continuous on the open domain.

[F5] [[thm-heine-borel-rn]]: closed bounded subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space are compact.

[F6] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]]: a boundary point $y\in\partial A_x$ has $A_y=A_x$; strict accessibility is interior membership. Together with [F2], this identifies entropy levels with sector boundaries.

[F7] [[lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation]]: T1 and the reversible-split existence in T2 force a common orientation sign; the common affine proof-coordinate change preserves all energy-sum joins and does not redefine physical energy.

## Proof

1.1 Use [F7]'s common mathematical energy orientation for the proof coordinates. Apply [F2] using [F1] after dividing represented coefficient maps by the fixed positive type weight $w_\Gamma$, as specified in [A1]. Multiply the resulting unit-state entropy by $w_\Gamma$ to evaluate represented states; this positive factor preserves all same-type order comparisons. Write $S(x)$ for that represented-state value. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] and additivity imply concavity: for $0<t<1$, accessibility of $(tx,(1-t)y)$ to $tx+(1-t)y$ gives $tS(x)+(1-t)S(y)\le S(tx+(1-t)y)$. By [F3], $S$ is strictly increasing in energy at fixed work coordinate. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F7]

1.2 Fix a work coordinate $v$ and let $J_v:=\{u:(u,v)\in\Gamma\}$, an open interval. The restriction $s_v(u)=S(u,v)$ is finite, concave, continuous by [F4], and strictly increasing by [F3]. For an interior $u$, concavity makes the right secant slopes nonincreasing as the secant endpoint moves right, and the left secant slopes monotone as the endpoint approaches $u$; hence the one-sided derivative limits $s'_{v,+}(u)$ and $s'_{v,-}(u)$ exist. Choose $a<u<b$ in $J_v$: the secants to $a,b$ bound those limits, so they are finite, and concavity gives $s'_-\ge s'_+$. Monotonicity gives nonnegative slopes. If $s'_+(u)=0$, then for every $z>u$ concavity bounds $(s_v(z)-s_v(u))/(z-u)\le s'_+(u)=0$, contradicting strict increase. Thus $s'_-\ge s'_+>0$. Define $\Theta(u,v)=[1/s'_{v,-}(u),1/s'_{v,+}(u)]$, a nonempty compact interval of positive finite reciprocal slopes. [A1, F3, F4, algebra]

1.3 Suppose the second alternative fails, so each adiabat contains one thermal-equivalence class. By [F1]–[F2], $A_x=\{y:S(y)\ge S(x)\}$. Continuity of $S$ and strict increase in energy at fixed work coordinate imply that every point with $S=\sigma$ has arbitrarily nearby points with larger and smaller entropy; hence each entropy level $E_\sigma=\{x:S(x)=\sigma\}$ is a forward-sector boundary. The supposition makes each $E_\sigma$ lie in one thermal class. Let $R=S(\Gamma)$ and, for each thermal class $C_\alpha$, put $R_\alpha=\{S(x):x\in C_\alpha\}$. These sets partition $R$: two distinct classes cannot share a level under the supposition. The range $R$ is an interval, since any two points of the convex domain are joined by a segment and the continuous entropy takes every intermediate value along it. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, F4, F6]

2.1 Fix $x=(u_1,v_1)$ and $y=(u_2,v_2)$ of this same simple type, and let $U=u_1+u_2$. The admissible energy splits form the open interval $D=\{w:(U-w,v_1)\in\Gamma,\ (w,v_2)\in\Gamma\}$, which contains $u_2$. Define $g(w)=s_{v_1}(U-w)+s_{v_2}(w)$. For the join state $J(x,y)$, T2 gives an admissible split $q$ whose pair is reversible with the join. For every other split $p$, T1 gives $p\prec J(x,y)\prec q$, so $p\prec q$. The pair states $p,q$ are finite compounds of two copies of this same simple type; [F1]–[F2] and their entropy representation therefore give $g(p)\le g(q)$. Thus $q$ maximizes $g$. If the initial split $x,y$ is reversible with the join, it is equivalent to $q$; entropy representation gives equal entropy, so it too maximizes $g$. Conversely, if $u_2$ maximizes $g$, then $g(u_2)=g(q)$, and [F1]–[F2] make the initial pair reversible with $q$; composing with $q\sim J(x,y)$ shows $x\sim_T y$. For a concave function at an interior point, maximality is equivalent to $g'_+(u_2)\le0\le g'_-(u_2)$: right secants are bounded above by the right derivative and left secants below by the left derivative. Here
$g'_+(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,+}(u_2),\qquad
g'_-(u_2)=-s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)+s'_{v_2,-}(u_2).$
The two inequalities are exactly $s'_{v_1,+}(u_1)\le s'_{v_2,-}(u_2)$ and $s'_{v_2,+}(u_2)\le s'_{v_1,-}(u_1)$, which say the positive slope intervals intersect; reciprocal reverses their endpoints, so this is equivalent to $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(y)\ne\varnothing$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 Let $T_\alpha$ be one thermal class. The compact intervals $\Theta(x)$, $x\in T_\alpha$, pairwise intersect by step 2.1. For any finite subfamily, pairwise intersection implies common intersection: the largest left endpoint is no greater than the smallest right endpoint, since the intervals attaining those two endpoints intersect. Fix $x_0\in T_\alpha$; the sets $\Theta(x)\cap\Theta(x_0)$ are closed subsets of the compact interval $\Theta(x_0)$ and have the finite-intersection property. Compactness [F5] gives a common point, so $I_\alpha:=\bigcap_{x\in T_\alpha}\Theta(x)$ is a nonempty compact interval. If distinct classes had intersecting common intervals, representatives $x,y$ would have intersecting $\Theta$ intervals and would be thermally equivalent by step 2.1, a contradiction. Thus the intervals $I_\alpha$ for distinct classes are disjoint and strictly ordered on the real line; use this as the order of the classes. [A2, F5, step 2.1]

4.1 For each work coordinate $v$, strict continuity of $s_v$ maps the open interval $J_v$ onto an open interval $R_v\subset R$. On $R_v$, the level-to-class map is nondecreasing: as $u$ increases, concavity makes both one-sided slopes nonincreasing, so both endpoints of $\Theta(u,v)$ are nondecreasing. If two such intervals $\Theta$ are disjoint, monotonicity of both endpoints forces the earlier interval to lie strictly below the later one; by step 3.1, this is the class order. The local class maps agree on overlaps of $R_v$ because each entropy level lies in one class. The open intervals $R_v$ cover $R$. Any compact subinterval of $R$ has a finite subcover by these intervals by [F5]; its intersection graph is connected, since otherwise the connected subinterval would be split into two disjoint nonempty relatively open sets. Chaining the local orders through overlaps proves that the class map is nondecreasing on all of $R$. [A1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 1.3, step 3.1]

5.1 Fix $\sigma\in R_\alpha$ and $x\in E_\sigma$. T4 gives $x_0\prec\prec x\prec\prec x_1$ with $x_0\sim_T x_1$. Entropy representation gives $S(x_0)<\sigma<S(x_1)$, and their levels belong to the same class $R_\alpha$. The global nondecreasing order from step 4.1 forces every level between them, including an open neighborhood of $\sigma$, into $R_\alpha$. Thus each class set is open in the interval $R$. Since these disjoint open sets partition connected $R$, only one nonempty class exists. Under the supposition, all states are thermally equivalent, proving the dichotomy. [A2, F2, step 4.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2$ be simple domains in a family of finite thermal joins satisfying A1–A7, S1–S3, T1–T5, and C1 of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]. Then there are $x_0\prec\prec x_1$ in $\Gamma_1$ and $y_0\prec\prec y_1$ in $\Gamma_2$ such that

$$(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0).$$

Moreover, for every fixed finite composition of scaled copies of $\Gamma_1$ and $\Gamma_2$, any two equal-mass states of that same composition are comparable (CH). The conclusion is conditional on the explicitly stated join-coherence and universal-range assumptions C1 and T5.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The forward-sector and contact hypotheses for the whole join-closed family.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: A1–A7 and S1–S3 hold on each member of the family, including finite joins.

[A2] [[def-tdmath-thermal-contact-hypotheses]]: T1–T5 hold for every ordered pair in the family, and C1 makes an equilibrated joined state thermally equivalent to each equilibrium constituent.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-reference-strip-gluing]]: CH holds on every finite scaled product of copies of any simple type in the family.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: under that CH, each simple type and its scaled products have an additive extensive entropy representing accessibility.

[F3] [[lem-tdmath-thermal-class-dichotomy]]: for each simple join, either every pair of its states is thermally equivalent or one of its adiabats contains two thermally inequivalent states.

[F4] [[thm-tdmath-sector-nesting]] and [[thm-tdmath-forward-boundary-graph]]: a common adiabat has identical forward sectors; fixed-work accessibility is ordered by energy, and each component adiabat has one state at each work coordinate in its projection.

[F5] [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]] and [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]]: signed equivalence is preserved by finite addition and cancellation of common spectators.

[F8] [[lem-tdmath-contact-energy-orientation]]: T1–T2 and arbitrary-spectator cancellation force a common mathematical energy orientation; the common affine change preserves the join energy-sum rule.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1]–[A2], [F1]–[F5], and [F8].

1.1 Work in [F8]'s common affine mathematical energy orientation, without redefining any physical energy or calibration. Apply [F1] and [F2] to each simple type, including every finite join, using the positive normalization by its fixed weight in [A1]. Throughout, entropy at a state means its represented-state value: $w_\Gamma$ times its unit-point-mass representation. This normalization preserves order and finite scalar amounts. The convex-combination access hypothesis in [A1] makes each resulting entropy concave, since the comparison of a scaled pair with its convex-combination state translates under the representation to the concavity inequality. By [F4], each entropy is strictly increasing with energy at fixed work coordinates. [A1, F1, F2, F4, F8]

1.2 Use T5 to choose $\bar x\in\Gamma_1$ and $\bar y\in\Gamma_2$ with $\bar x\sim_T\bar y$. Let $\phi=J_{12}(\bar x,\bar y)$ and consider its adiabat $\partial A_\phi$. T2 gives every $Z$ on that adiabat at least one split $Z=J_{12}(x_Z,y_Z)$ with $x_Z\sim_T y_Z$. [A2, F4, choose]

2.1 Suppose a join state $Z$ on $\partial A_\phi$ has two distinct equilibrium splits $(x^{(1)},y^{(1)})$ and $(x^{(2)},y^{(2)})$. By the definition of $\sim_T$, both pairs are reversible with $Z$, hence mutually accessible compounds. Their work coordinates are fixed by $Z$ and their total energies equal its energy. If the first-component energies agreed, both component states in the splits would agree, so distinctness forces unequal first-component energies. If $u_{x^{(1)}}<u_{x^{(2)}}$, fixed-work comparison [F4] gives $x^{(1)}\prec\prec x^{(2)}$; conservation of total energy gives $u_{y^{(2)}}<u_{y^{(1)}}$, hence $y^{(2)}\prec\prec y^{(1)}$. Taking $(x_0,x_1,y_0,y_1)=(x^{(1)},x^{(2)},y^{(2)},y^{(1)})$ gives $(x_0,y_1)\sim(x_1,y_0)$ because both split compounds are reversible with $Z$. If the first energies occur in the opposite order, swap the two splits and obtain the same calibrator form. Therefore, if no calibrator exists, every $Z\in\partial A_\phi$ has a unique equilibrium split. [A2, F4, step 1.2, choose]

3.1 Assume no calibrator exists. For any equilibrium split $(x_Z,y_Z)$ of $Z\in\partial A_\phi$, reversibility with $Z$ and the common adiabat give $(x_Z,y_Z)\sim(\bar x,\bar y)$ as compounds. By [F1], $x_Z$ and $\bar x$ are comparable; [F4] says their sectors coincide exactly when they are equivalent. If $x_Z\prec\prec\bar x$, pair reversibility gives $(\bar x,\bar y)\prec(x_Z,y_Z)$. Consistency adds $\bar y$ to $x_Z\prec\bar x$, and cancellation [F5] gives $\bar y\prec y_Z$. If $y_Z\prec\bar y$, consistency and the pair comparison instead cancel to give $\bar x\prec x_Z$, a contradiction. Thus $\bar y\prec\prec y_Z$, making a calibrator. The case $\bar x\prec\prec x_Z$ is symmetric: it gives $y_Z\prec\prec\bar y$, again a calibrator. Since neither is allowed under the assumption, $x_Z\sim\bar x$. Adding spectators to the two directions and cancelling by [F5] then gives both $\bar y\prec y_Z$ and $y_Z\prec\bar y$, so $y_Z\sim\bar y$. Thus every split on this adiabat has components in the corresponding component adiabats. [A1, A2, F1, F4, F5, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Under the no-calibrator assumption, fix a first-component work coordinate $v_1$ in the projection of $\partial A_{\bar x}$. The boundary-graph result [F4] gives exactly one state $x_*$ on that component adiabat at $v_1$. Every split of a join state on $\partial A_\phi$ with first work coordinate $v_1$ therefore has first component $x_*$. Each split is thermal, so $x_*\sim_T y_Z$ for its second component. T3 makes all such $y_Z$ thermally equivalent, and C1 makes each joined state $J(x_*,y_Z)=Z$ thermally equivalent to $x_*$. Hence all join states on this adiabat over fixed $v_1$ lie in one thermal class. Fixing a second-component work coordinate instead gives the corresponding conclusion for first components. [A2, F4, step 3.1]

5.1 Let $\Omega$ be the open connected work-coordinate projection of $\partial A_\phi$ from [F4]. From any point of $\Omega$, the set reachable by finitely many coordinate-axis segments contained in open boxes in $\Omega$ is relatively open, and its complement is also relatively open; connectedness makes the reachable set all of $\Omega$. Along each such segment, step 4.1 gives equivalence of the corresponding join states; T3 composes these finitely many equivalences. Thus the whole adiabat $\partial A_\phi$ is one thermal class. Since the argument works for every starting join state, every join adiabat is one thermal class. [A2, F4, step 4.1, construct]

6.1 Still assuming no calibrator, apply [F3] to each join system. Its alternative with two thermally inequivalent states on one adiabat is excluded by step 5.1, so all states of each join system are thermally equivalent. For any $x,x'\in\Gamma_1$, use T5 with one allowed second work coordinate to choose $y,y'$ with $x\sim_T y$ and $x'\sim_T y'$. C1 relates each component to its joined state, and all join states are in one thermal class; T3 therefore gives $x\sim_T x'$. The same argument gives one thermal class in $\Gamma_2$. Now take $Z=\phi\in\partial A_\phi$ and a split $(x,y)$ supplied by T2. Choose nonzero sufficiently small $\delta$ so $(u_x+\delta,v_1)\in\Gamma_1$ and $(u_y-\delta,v_2)\in\Gamma_2$, possible because the domains are open. These states form a distinct split of the same $Z$. Since the original split has $x\sim_T y$ and each component type is one thermal class, T3 gives thermal equivalence of the changed pair as well. This contradicts uniqueness of the split from step 2.1. Therefore a calibrator exists. [A2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 5.1, choose]

7.1 Fix a calibrator $x_0\prec\prec x_1$, $y_0\prec\prec y_1$, whose existence is step 6.1. Choose same-type entropy representatives $S_1,S_2$ from [F2], with positive gaps $h_1=S_1(x_1)-S_1(x_0)$ and $h_2=S_2(y_1)-S_2(y_0)$. Normalize $\widetilde S_i=S_i/h_i$, so both calibrator increments are one, and put $s(x)=\widetilde S_1(x)-\widetilde S_1(x_0)$ and $t(y)=\widetilde S_2(y)-\widetilde S_2(y_0)$. Write $u=\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_1)$ and $v=\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_0)$. The calibrator says $u\sim v$, so $v-u=(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$ is equivalent to zero; translation and cancellation [F5] give $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$. For any state $x$, the signed map $d_x=\mathsf{J}(x)-(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)-s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ has total mass and $\widetilde S_1$-value zero. Its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy, so [F2] makes them equivalent. Hence $\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s(x))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+s(x)\mathsf{J}(x_1)$; the same argument applies to states of the second type. These are formal signed maps when a coefficient lies outside $[0,1]$. [F2, F5, step 6.1, algebra]

8.1 For a state pair $(x,y)$, put $\lambda=(s(x)+t(y))/2$ and $\delta=(s(x)-t(y))/2$. Adding the signed reductions from step 7.1 makes the pair equivalent to $(1-\lambda)(\mathsf{J}(x_0)+\mathsf{J}(y_0))+\lambda(\mathsf{J}(x_1)+\mathsf{J}(y_1))$ plus $\delta[(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))-(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))]$. The calibrator increment equivalence from step 7.1 makes the latter term equivalent to zero for either sign of $\delta$. Thus each pair reduces to its reference map at parameter $\lambda$. For any finite compound $A$ with amounts $M_1,M_2$ of the two types, add and scale these single-state reductions. Writing $q_1(A),q_2(A)$ for the amount-weighted sums of $s(x),t(y)$, respectively, gives $A\sim_s(M_1-q_1(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)+q_1(A)\mathsf{J}(x_1)+(M_2-q_2(A))\mathsf{J}(y_0)+q_2(A)\mathsf{J}(y_1)$. Using $(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(y_1)-\mathsf{J}(y_0))$, this is equivalent to $M_1\mathsf{J}(x_0)+M_2\mathsf{J}(y_0)+Q(A)(\mathsf{J}(x_1)-\mathsf{J}(x_0))$, where $Q(A)=q_1(A)+q_2(A)$. If the total mass is zero, both compounds are empty and reflexivity compares them. Otherwise, for same-composition $A,B$, their base terms agree. If $Q(A)<Q(B)$, the positive and negative parts of the reference-map difference are $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_1)$ and $(Q(B)-Q(A))\mathsf{J}(x_0)$, so $x_0\prec x_1$ and positive scaling compares the maps forward. If the Q values agree the maps coincide; if $Q(A)>Q(B)$ the reverse comparison holds. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F5] transfer the result to $A,B$. This proves CH for every fixed finite composition of the two types and their scaled copies. [A1, F2, F5, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The proof uses C1 in steps 4.1 and 6.1 and T5 in steps 1.2 and 6.1. It does not establish the calibrator from the bare set-valued join formula or from T1–T4 alone. All conclusions remain conditional mathematical consequences of the listed hypotheses.

## Statement

Let $I$ be a nonempty set of primitive simple-system labels containing a distinguished meter label $m$. Assume every finite separated product is explicitly represented by its finitely many tagged elementary factors; positive scaling and finite product are the only identifications. Suppose the join-closed family satisfies the hypotheses of [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]], and fix a strict meter pair $z_0\prec\prec z_1$ in $\Gamma_m$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Then one can choose, for every $i\in I$, an additive constant and positive scale for its same-type entropy so that

$$S\big((t_1i_1,x_1),\ldots,(t_ni_n,x_n)\big)=\sum_{\ell=1}^n t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$$

is additive, extensive, and characterizes every same-composition comparison on every finite separated product. No conclusion is asserted for transitions that change composition.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The explicit finite-factor family, common contact branch, strict meter pair, and Axiom of Choice.

[A1] [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets admits a choice function; it selects the reference states, entropy representatives, and calibrator data used below.

[F1] [[thm-tdmath-conditional-contact-calibrator]]: for each pair of simple types in the join-closed family, strict calibrator endpoints exist and their reversible pair relation identifies the two reference increments in signed comparison.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-additive-entropy-representation]]: once a type and its scaled products have CH, a finite real additive extensive entropy represents their equal-mass comparisons.

[F3] [[def-tdmath-forward-signed-comparison]] and [[lem-tdmath-forward-spectator-cancellation]]: signed comparison is translation-invariant and additive, agrees with ordinary comparison on nonnegative equal-mass maps, and permits common-spectator cancellation.

## Proof

**Given:** [A1], [F1]–[F3].

1.1 Use the positive type normalization in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] whenever invoking [F2]; state entropies evaluate represented maps $\mathsf{J}(x)$, and their unit-label entropy density is $S_i(x)/w_{\Gamma_i}$. Apply [F2] to the meter type and choose its entropy $S_m$ so $S_m(z_0)=0$ and $S_m(z_1)=1$. Set the meter reference to $r_m=z_0$, and use [A1] to choose a reference state $r_i$ and one same-type entropy representative for every $i\ne m$. For each $i\ne m$, use [F1] to choose calibrator states $a_i,b_i\in\Gamma_i$ and $c_i,d_i\in\Gamma_m$ such that $a_i\prec\prec b_i$, $c_i\prec\prec d_i$, and $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$; also choose $r_i\in\Gamma_i$. For the meter label set $a_m=c_m=z_0$ and $b_m=d_m=z_1$; the two pairs $(z_0,z_1)$ and $(z_1,z_0)$ are the same two-copy meter compound up to permutation. Write $S_i^0$ for the selected entropy representative, with $S_m^0=S_m$, and put $\Delta_i=S_i^0(b_i)-S_i^0(a_i)>0$ and $\mu_i=S_m(d_i)-S_m(c_i)>0$. Define $S_i(x):=\frac{\mu_i}{\Delta_i}\bigl(S_i^0(x)-S_i^0(r_i)\bigr)$. Then $S_i(r_i)=0$ and $S_i(b_i)-S_i(a_i)=\mu_i$, matching the meter entropy increment across the chosen calibrator endpoints. For $i=m$, $\Delta_m=\mu_m=1$, so this agrees with the fixed meter normalization. [A1, F1, F2, choose]

2.1 For a finite separated compound $A$ with factors $(t_\ell i_\ell,x_\ell)$, define $S(A):=\sum_\ell t_\ell S_{i_\ell}(x_\ell)$. The sum is finite and invariant under reordering; concatenating compounds adds the sums, and scaling every amount by $t>0$ multiplies it by $t$. The explicit-factor convention in the Statement therefore makes $S$ well-defined, additive, and extensive. [A1, step 1.1, construct]

3.1 Fix a composition with amounts $M_i$ for finitely many labels and let $A,B$ be two states of that same composition. For a state $x$ of type $i$, put
$s_i(x):=\frac{S_i(x)-S_i(a_i)}{\mu_i}.$
The same-type entropy representation and the CH for type $i$ show
$\mathsf{J}(x)\sim_s(1-s_i(x))\mathsf{J}(a_i)+s_i(x)\mathsf{J}(b_i).$
Indeed, the signed difference has total coefficient zero and $S_i$-value zero, so its positive and negative parts have equal mass and entropy and therefore compare both ways by [F2]. The calibrator relation gives
$(\mathsf{J}(b_i)-\mathsf{J}(a_i))\sim_s(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i))$
by taking the signed difference of $(a_i,d_i)\sim(b_i,c_i)$ and canceling common terms with [F3]. Add and scale these identities over the finitely many factors of $A$. With
$q_i(A):=\sum_{\ell:\,i_\ell=i}t_\ell s_i(x_\ell),$
the resulting signed map is
$A\sim_s \sum_i M_i \mathsf{J}(a_i)+\sum_i q_i(A)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)),$
where the sums range over the finite support of the composition. The same holds for $B$. Since they have the same composition, the reference base cancels, and $B-A$ is signed-equivalent to the finite meter map
$D:=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)(\mathsf{J}(d_i)-\mathsf{J}(c_i)).$
Extend the meter entropy linearly to raw finite signed coefficient maps using density $S_m(z)/w_{\Gamma_m}$ at a meter raw tag $(\Gamma_m,z)$; in particular its value on $\mathsf{J}(z)$ is $S_m(z)$. Then
$S_m(D)=\sum_i\bigl(q_i(B)-q_i(A)\bigr)\mu_i=S(B)-S(A).$
The positive and negative parts of $D$ have equal mass. If $S(A)\le S(B)$, the same-type entropy representation [F2] for finite meter products gives $D^-\prec D^+$, hence $D$ compares in the forward signed direction. Translation, addition, and ordinary-order compatibility [F3] transfer this to $A\prec B$. Conversely, if $A\prec B$, the same signed equivalences and translation in [F3] give $D^-\prec D^+$. The meter representation in [F2] then forces $S_m(D)=S(B)-S(A)\ge0$. Reversing the entropy inequality gives the reverse comparison. Thus $S$ characterizes every same-composition comparison. Each particular comparison uses only finitely many labels; no infinite sum or uncountable product occurs. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The meter normalization fixes the multiplicative unit. Changing the chosen reference state for type $i$ changes only its additive constant; on a finite compound these constants contribute amount-weighted conserved-type offsets. This proves the stated freedom and completes the construction. [A1, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎
## Remarks

AC is used only for simultaneous reference-state, entropy-representative, and calibrator choices over the arbitrary label set $I$. Cross-composition monotonicity requires the additional cost and offset hypotheses developed later.

## Definition

Let $\mathcal G$ be a set of tagged system types closed under finite composition $T\times T'$ and positive scaling $tT$. Scaling is associative and acts componentwise on products: $s(tT)=(st)T$ and $t(T\times T')=(tT)\times(tT')$. Each type $T$ has a nonempty state set $X_T$ of finite tagged compounds, every state in $X_T$ is represented by the coefficient-map interpretation of [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]] and has the fixed aggregate composition $\nu(a)=\nu_T$ of its declared type, using the amount-function interpretation in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], and has total coefficient mass $m(T)=w_T\ge0$, and $\nu_{T\times T'}=\nu_T+\nu_{T'}$, $\nu_{tT}=t\nu_T$, with $m(T\times T')=m(T)+m(T')$ and $m(tT)=t\,m(T)$. Matching scalar masses alone do not identify aggregate composition. The entropy $\sigma_T:X_T\to\mathbb R$ is the finite additive extensive entropy from [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]; in particular $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$.

For each pair of types prescribe the product map $\pi_{T,T\prime}:X_T\times X_{T\prime}\to X_{T\times T\prime}$ by $\pi(a,b)=a+b$ on represented coefficient maps, and require it to be surjective: $X_{T\times T\prime}=\{a+b:a\in X_T,b\in X_{T\prime}\}$. Thus each product state admits a factorization, without requiring it to be unique. For $t>0$, prescribe the scaling bijection $s_{t,T}:X_T\to X_{tT}$ by $s_{t,T}(a)=ta$, with inverse coefficient scaling by $1/t$. The type identifications and the precise commuting conditions are specified below. Require $\sigma_{T\times T\prime}(a+b)=\sigma_T(a)+\sigma_{T\prime}(b)$ and $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$; entropy is therefore independent of any nonunique product factorization. Include the formal empty unit type $1$, with $X_1=\{0\}$, where $0$ is the empty coefficient map, $m(1)=0$, $\sigma_1(0)=0$, $T\times1=T$, and $t1=1$. A transition edge from type $T$ to type $T'$ is a pair $a\in X_T$, $b\in X_{T'}$ such that the underlying equal-mass compounds satisfy $a\prec b$ under [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]. Thus an edge can exist only when $m(T)=m(T')$. Its cost is the finite real number $\sigma_{T'}(b)-\sigma_T(a)$.

A decorated finite chain from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ consists of a catalyst type $C\in\mathcal G$, an integer $N\ge1$, types $T_0=\Gamma\times C,T_1,\ldots,T_N=\Gamma'\times C$, and states $a_k\in X_{T_k}$, $b_{k+1}\in X_{T_{k+1}}$ with an edge $a_k\prec b_{k+1}$ for every $0\le k<N$. Its cost is the finite real sum

$$c=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\bigl(\sigma_{T_{k+1}}(b_{k+1})-\sigma_{T_k}(a_k)\bigr).$$

Define the ordered extended real line $\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ by placing $-\infty$ below every real and $+\infty$ above every real. Finite addition retains its usual meaning; a real added to either infinity leaves that infinity, and equal-sign infinities add to themselves. Opposite-sign infinite sums are undefined. Positive multiplication preserves each infinity, and negation exchanges the infinities. For a nonempty real set bounded below, its infimum is its greatest real lower bound; completeness ensures existence. Define $F:\mathcal G\times\mathcal G\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ by taking $F(\Gamma,\Gamma\prime)$ as the infimum of all such witness costs. Set $F=+\infty$ if there is no witness and $F=-\infty$ if the witness costs are unbounded below. The infimum is over real witness costs, so no subtraction of extended-real infima is used. The structural identifications are product permutation and reassociation, $T\times1=T$, $1T=T$, $s(tT)=(st)T$, $t(T\times R)=(tT)\times(tR)$ and $t1=1$. Their state maps are the identity on the corresponding represented coefficient maps: finite addition is commutative and associative, adds zero for the unit, and commutes with coefficient scaling. Thus the displayed product and scaling maps commute with these identifications, which preserve $\nu$, $m$, $\sigma$ and accessibility.

Additional reversible identifications, if used, are separate specified data: a set $E\subseteq\mathcal G^2$ of pairs $(T,R)$ with $\nu_T=\nu_R$ and, for each pair, a bijection $r_{T,R}:X_T\to X_R$ such that $\sigma_R(r_{T,R}(a))=\sigma_T(a)$ and $a\sim r_{T,R}(a)$ for every $a\in X_T$. Include identity pairs with identity maps and close these data under inverse and composition, with $r_{R,T}=r_{T,R}^{-1}$ and $r_{R,H}\circ r_{T,R}=r_{T,H}$. Require closure under positive scaling and product with another specified pair $(D,H)$, with $r_{tT,tR}(ta)=t r_{T,R}(a)$ and $r_{T\times D,R\times H}(a+d)=r_{T,R}(a)+r_{D,H}(d)$. The latter must hold independently of every nonunique product factorization. These requirements give exactly the commuting product/scaling diagrams. They preserve aggregate composition and mass; replacing a state by its image preserves and reflects every comparison with any compound, by mutual accessibility, consistency and transitivity. Their maps and all structural maps must agree on overlapping identifications. One may take only the structural data, with no additional pairs. The calibration theorem does not supply additional identifications: these are hypotheses to check whenever chosen. Reversible equal-state splitting is an accessibility assertion; it does not identify every state of a product with a single unsplit state. The cost identities and inequalities require a separate proof.

## Definition

A cross-type mixing and reaction network consists of a declared set $\mathcal G$ of tagged composition types and a state set $X_\Gamma$ for each type. Each state set comes with a fixed formal composition $\nu_\Gamma$, and its states satisfy $\nu(x)=\nu_\Gamma$ as in [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. These mathematical coefficients and their positive type weights are distinct from dimensioned material amounts. For physical channels the model additionally supplies endpoint quantity maps $U_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ and $n_\Gamma:X_\Gamma\to\mathbb R^r\,\mathrm{mol}$ in a declared finite species list, together with any separately tracked mechanical or external-field endpoint quantities. No identification of two distinct scaled tags is made.

For each channel $\alpha$ from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$, the model supplies sets $Z_\alpha$ of configurations, $\mathcal K_\alpha$ of protocol records, $\mathcal B_\alpha$ of outer-boundary records, and $\mathcal R_\alpha$ of transfer records, and equilibrium subsets and endpoint maps $\xi^-_\alpha:Z^-_\alpha\to X_\Gamma$, $\xi^+_\alpha:Z^+_\alpha\to X_{\Gamma'}$. A typed record is
$$P=(I,x^-,x^+,z,\kappa,b,r),$$
where $I=[t_0,t_1]$, $t_0<t_1$, is a finite time interval in seconds, $x^-\in X_\Gamma$, $x^+\in X_{\Gamma'}$, $z:I\to Z_\alpha$, $z(t_0)\in Z^-_\alpha$, $z(t_1)\in Z^+_\alpha$, $\xi^-_\alpha(z(t_0))=x^-$, $\xi^+_\alpha(z(t_1))=x^+$, $\kappa\in\mathcal K_\alpha$, $b\in\mathcal B_\alpha$, and $r\in\mathcal R_\alpha$. Write $\mathcal T_\alpha$ for this typed record set. Transfer maps $Q_\alpha,W_{\mathrm{on},\alpha}:\mathcal T_\alpha\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ and $N_\alpha:\mathcal T_\alpha\to\mathbb R^r\,\mathrm{mol}$ record heat, work and material transfer with declared signs; any tracked $\Delta K_{\mathrm{cm}}$ and $\Delta U_{\mathrm{ext}}$ are also joule-valued record maps. The transfer maps may depend on the whole record; factorization through the field $r$ requires an additional declared condition. The channel specifies a balance predicate on $\mathcal T_\alpha$, or equivalently a balance map into a declared product of quantity spaces whose required value is zero, and a model-admitted subset satisfying that predicate. The predicate states the actual energy and material constraints of that channel; no balance law, physical admission or endpoint realizability follows from the tuple alone. Other channels require their own adopted constraints. Define $(\Gamma,x)\mathcal R(\Gamma',y)$ exactly when an admitted channel record has those endpoints. No channel is inferred from separated composition.

For a fixed-constitution core closed channel of system $s$, use $X_\Gamma=X_{\Gamma'}=D_c$ and all six original fields, configuration/equilibrium sets and endpoint maps of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. Fix the outer-boundary record $b_s$ of that system and take $\mathcal B_\alpha=\{b_s\}$. The embedding

$$\iota_s(I,x^-,x^+,z,\kappa,r)=(I,x^-,x^+,z,\kappa,b_s,r)$$

is a bijection from $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ onto the core channel's admitted subset; its inverse deletes the fixed field $b_s$. Thus the subsets are identified by this map, not by equality of six- and seven-tuples. On the image assign $Q_\alpha(\iota_s(P))=Q[P](1\,\mathrm J)$ and $W_{\mathrm{on},\alpha}(\iota_s(P))=W_{\mathrm{on}}[P](1\,\mathrm J)$, where the supplier's real values are numerical joule values. Set $N_\alpha=0$ there and retain the supplier's stronger no-matter-crossing condition throughout the interval, together with its fixed-chart mass, endpoint velocities and zero kinetic/external changes. These assignments need not factor through $r$ alone. Values on other typed records are separate protocol data and do not enlarge the admitted subset or assert an energy-balance law.

For any permitted equal-formal-mass compound states $A,B$ of the network, define $A\prec B$ exactly when at least one admitted channel record has initial state $A$ and final state $B$; for named single types this is the relation $\mathcal R$ above. This is the exact relation supplied to [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], not a separate abstract order that enlarges or restricts the channel edges. Its extension to finite tagged products and common spectators is governed by the adopted A1–A6 conditions below. Thus every edge in a decorated chain is precisely an admitted channel transition. This identification is a declared model condition.

The network is **finite-factor closed** when its types admit the declared finite composition and positive scaling operations and each allowed channel respects the model’s stated conservation constraints. In this network class, explicitly adopt the represented state-family conditions of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]. Each $X_T$ is a nonempty set of finite coefficient-map states with its declared fixed $\nu_T$. The separated-product map

$$\pi_{T,T\prime}:X_T\times X_{T\prime}\to X_{T\times T\prime},\qquad \pi_{T,T\prime}(a,b)=a+b$$

is surjective, so each admitted separated-product state has a factorization, which need not be unique. For every $t>0$, the positive coefficient-scaling map $s_{t,T}:X_T\to X_{tT}$, $s_{t,T}(a)=ta$, is a bijection with inverse scaling by $1/t$. These maps commute with the declared reassociation, permutation and scaling conventions and preserve the exact amount-function and formal-mass identities. The empty unit has $X_1=\{0\}$ with the empty coefficient map $0$. A chosen finite real baseline entropy family used for the chain costs must obey

$$\sigma_{T\times T\prime}(a+b)=\sigma_T(a)+\sigma_{T\prime}(b),\qquad \sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a),\qquad \sigma_1(0)=0,$$

independently of a nonunique factorization. These are explicit admissibility and calibration conditions of the declared model, not consequences of a channel record or claims that every physical network satisfies them. Separated products remain sums of represented states; the distinct raw tags of scaled and joined types are retained, with reversible preparation transport as specified in [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]], rather than identifying those tags. The dimensioned endpoint-quantity maps and channel balance predicates remain the separately supplied physical data. In addition, each channel must preserve the dimensionless formal mass $m$ of [[def-td-scaled-products-and-comparison]]; this is the equal-coefficient-mass convention required by the mathematical chain-cost supplier, not a statement that formal mass is kilograms or moles. The common relation on all equal-formal-mass compounds satisfies A1–A6 of [[post-td-accessibility-a1-a6]], including consistency with spectators and stability. A decorated finite chain is exactly a finite sequence of such allowed transitions with a common catalyst and the real baseline-entropy edge costs in [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]].

For $\Gamma,\Gamma'$, let $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}$ be the infimum of those finite decorated-chain costs, with $+\infty$ if no witness exists and $-\infty$ if costs are unbounded below. The network has **no sinks** when, for every ordered type pair,

$$F(\Gamma,\Gamma')<+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F(\Gamma',\Gamma)<+\infty.$$

No-sinks is an explicit property required of a network used in the global-offset theorem; it is not proved by this definition, and it is not asserted for every physical mixing or reaction. Raw channel data may have an empty channel set, but such data do not satisfy the finite-factor-closed A1–A6 subclass above: each nonempty $X_T$ requires an admitted identity-endpoint witness by A1. ## Definition

A finite rate model consists of a finite nonempty state set $S$ and rates $q_{ij}\ge0$ in seconds$^{-1}$ for $i\ne j$. Set $q_{ii}=-\sum_{j\ne i}q_{ij}$. A row probability vector is $p=(p_i)_{i\in S}$ with $p_i\ge0$ and $\sum_i p_i=1$; write $\Delta(S)=\{p\in[0,1]^S:\sum_i p_i=1\}$. A time-dependent law is a coordinatewise continuously differentiable map $p:[0,\infty)\to\Delta(S)$, with a right derivative at $t=0$, that satisfies the continuous-time master equation $\dot p_i(t)=\sum_{j\ne i}[p_j(t)q_{ji}-p_i(t)q_{ij}]$ for every $t\ge0$. A strictly positive normalized vector $\pi$ is a detailed-balance law when $\pi_iq_{ij}=\pi_jq_{ji}$ for every distinct pair. Its undirected rate graph has an edge $\{i,j\}$ exactly when $\pi_iq_{ij}>0$; detailed balance makes this equivalent to $\pi_jq_{ji}>0$.

On a finite nonempty state set $S$, a discrete transition kernel is a matrix $K:S\times S\to[0,1]$ satisfying $\sum_{j\in S}K(i,j)=1$ for every $i\in S$. For a strictly positive row probability vector $\pi\in\Delta(S)$, the kernel satisfies $\pi$-detailed balance when $\pi_iK(i,j)=\pi_jK(j,i)$ for every $i,j\in S$. This identity pairs the supports of forward and reversed transitions. A rate model or a reversible kernel is a mathematical/physical model class; no observed trajectory is asserted by the definition.

## Definition

## Statement

Let $M$ and $R$ take values in finite sets under a joint probability law $p(m,r)\ge0$ with $\sum_{m,r}p(m,r)=1$. For any finite random variable $Y$ with law $p_Y$, define its Shannon entropy by $H(Y):=-\sum_{y:p_Y(y)>0}p_Y(y)\log p_Y(y)$; for a pair, $H(M,R)$ means this definition applied to its joint law. Put $a_r:=\sum_m p(m,r)$ and, when $a_r>0$, $q(m|r):=p(m,r)/a_r$. Thus $H(R)=-\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r\log a_r$. Define $H(M|R):=\sum_{r:a_r>0}a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Then $H(M,R)=H(R)+H(M|R)$ and $H(M|R)\ge0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** As stated in the item.

[A1] $M,R$ take values in finite sets under the joint probability law $p(m,r)$.

[F1] [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]] and [[def-finite-sum]]: joint weights are nonnegative and sum to one, and all displayed sums are finite.

[F2] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: logarithms of positive products add, $\log 1=0$, and $\log x\le0$ for $0<x\le1$.

## Proof

**Given:** A finite joint probability law for $M$ and $R$.

1.1 For every $r$ with $a_r>0$, the numbers $q(m|r)$ are nonnegative and sum to one. The joint identity $p(m,r)=a_rq(m|r)$ on positive entries gives $\log p(m,r)=\log a_r+\log q(m|r)$; summing $-p\log p$ over each fixed $r$ yields $-a_r\log a_r+a_r[-\sum_{m:q(m|r)>0}q(m|r)\log q(m|r)]$. Terms with $a_r=0$ have all $p(m,r)=0$ and contribute nothing. Summing over finite $r$ proves the chain rule. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 For each positive conditional probability $q(m|r)\le1$, [F2] gives $-q(m|r)\log q(m|r)\ge0$. Multiplying by $a_r\ge0$ and summing proves $H(M|R)\ge0$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1] ∎

Fix $d\ge2$. The **elastic collision set** is
$$Q_{\rm el}:=\{(v,w,v',w')\in\mathbb R^{4d}:v+w=v'+w',\ |v|^2+|w|^2=|v'|^2+|w'|^2\},$$
with its relative Borel sigma-algebra. A collision measure is a nonnegative countably additive measure $\nu$ on this measurable space. It is symmetric if it is invariant under the exchanges $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(w,v)$, $(v',w')\leftrightarrow(w',v')$, and $(v,w)\leftrightarrow(v',w')$. These invariances are hypotheses on $\nu$, not consequences of energy and momentum conservation.

Fix the velocity measure space $(\mathbb R^d,\mathcal L(\mathbb R^d),dv)$, where $dv$ is the Lebesgue set function of [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]] and its countably additive measure-space structure is assumed as part of the data. This definition makes no existence assertion for that structure or for the collision operator. An input density is a finite-valued positive Lebesgue-measurable function $f:\mathbb R^d\to(0,\infty)$ whose four coordinate evaluations $f(v),f(w),f(v'),f(w')$ on $Q_{\rm el}$ are $\nu$-measurable. Let $\mathcal D_\nu$ be a declared set of such inputs. Put $\mathcal L^1_{\rm loc}:=\{q:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R:q\text{ is Lebesgue measurable and }\int_K|q|\,dv<\infty\text{ for every compact }K\subset\mathbb R^d\}$. Its elements here are chosen function representatives, rather than equivalence classes. A collision model includes a specified map $Q_\nu:\mathcal D_\nu\to\mathcal L^1_{\rm loc}$; write $Q(f):=Q_\nu(f)$.

For $f\in\mathcal D_\nu$, put $A=f(v)f(w)$ and $B=f(v')f(w')$. For a finite-valued complex Lebesgue-measurable function $\varphi$ on velocity space, put $\delta\varphi:=\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w')$. Define the complete admissible test class $\mathcal T_f$ to consist of exactly those $\varphi$ for which $\delta\varphi$ is $\nu$-measurable and
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}|\varphi(v)Q_\nu(f)(v)|\,dv<\infty,\qquad \int_{Q_{\rm el}}|(B-A)\delta\varphi|\,d\nu<\infty.$$
Absolute integrability is in the sense of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. The model also declares, for each $f\in\mathcal D_\nu$, a complex linear testing subspace $\mathcal S_f\subseteq\mathcal T_f$ containing at least one nonzero test. Require the following **weak collision identity** for every $f\in\mathcal D_\nu$ and every $\varphi\in\mathcal S_f$. A formulation adopting all admissible tests specifies $\mathcal S_f=\mathcal T_f$; a result using only particular tests names those tests and their linear span explicitly:
$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\varphi(v)Q(f)(v)\,dv=\frac14\int_{Q_{\rm el}}(f(v')f(w')-f(v)f(w))(\varphi(v)+\varphi(w)-\varphi(v')-\varphi(w'))\,d\nu,$$

Admissible tests need not be bounded or compactly supported: $1$, velocity coordinates, squared speed, and $\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$ for a positive constant $f_{\rm ref}$ belong to $\mathcal T_f$ whenever they meet the displayed measurability and integrability conditions. In particular, the entropy branch uses the span of $1$ and $\log(f/f_{\rm ref})$, with absolute convergence explicitly assumed. The map $Q_\nu$, its input domain and its testing domains are adopted model data; the weak identity is their admissibility condition, not an assertion that every positive density and collision measure admit such a map or that these tests alone uniquely determine it. Molecular chaos or a microscopic derivation of the identity is not part of the definition.

## Definition

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix an integer $n\ge1$ and an open phase-coordinate domain $O_{\rm phys}\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ with physical canonical coordinates $q_i$ in metres and $p_i$ in $\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}}$. The canonical symplectic form on this chart is $\omega_{\rm phys}=\sum_{i=1}^n dq_i\wedge dp_i$. Let $\hat q_i=q_i/(1\,\mathrm m)$ and $\hat p_i=p_i/(1\,\mathrm{kg\,m\,s^{-1}})$, and let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{2n}$ be the open image of the chart in these dimensionless coordinates. The corresponding dimensionless canonical form is $\hat\omega=\sum_{i=1}^n d\hat q_i\wedge d\hat p_i$, so $\omega_{\rm phys}=(1\,\mathrm{J\,s})\hat\omega$.

Let $\hat H:O\to\mathbb R$ be a numerical energy function with continuous partial derivatives through order two, and let $H_{\rm phys}:O_{\rm phys}\to\mathbb R\,\mathrm J$ be $H_{\rm phys}(q,p)=(1\,\mathrm J)\hat H(\hat q,\hat p)$. Where defined, its physical Hamiltonian vector field $X_{H_{\rm phys}}$ is determined by $\iota_{X_{H_{\rm phys}}}\omega_{\rm phys}=dH_{\rm phys}$. For each elapsed time $t$ in its domain, the physical flow map is a function $\phi_t:D_t\to O_{\rm phys}$, where $D_t\subseteq O_{\rm phys}$ is the set of initial data whose trajectories exist through time $t$, and it satisfies $d\phi_t/dt=X_{H_{\rm phys}}\circ\phi_t$. Equivalently, in the dimensionless chart, the flow map $\hat\phi_{\hat t}:\hat D_{\hat t}\to O$ is generated by $X_{\hat H}$ satisfying $\iota_{X_{\hat H}}\hat\omega=d\hat H$, at dimensionless time $\hat t=t/(1\,\mathrm s)$; here $\hat D_{\hat t}$ is the set of initial coordinates whose trajectories exist through $\hat t$. These definitions specify the flow maps when they exist but impose no global-existence or completeness hypothesis on the shell preparation.

A specified open interval $J_E\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a regular compact-shell band when $\hat H^{-1}(K)$ is compact in $O$ for every compact $K\subset J_E$ and $\nabla\hat H$ is nonzero at every point of $\hat H^{-1}(J_E)$.

For $\hat E\in J_E$, the energy shell is $\Sigma_{\hat E}:=\{x\in O:\hat H(x)=\hat E\}$. The graph-chart definition of the weighted shell integral is [[def-tdmath-regular-energy-shell]]: in a local graph chart $x_i=h(z,\hat E)$, its coarea measure is $d\mu_{\hat E}=dA_{\hat E}/|\nabla\hat H|$, with graph-area factor and gradient in the dimensionless Euclidean coordinates. Set $D(\hat E):=\int_{\Sigma_{\hat E}}d\mu_{\hat E}$ and admit the preparation only when $\Sigma_{\hat E}\ne\varnothing$ and $0<D(\hat E)<\infty$. Its normalized shell law is $\nu_{\hat E}(A):=D(\hat E)^{-1}\mu_{\hat E}(A\cap\Sigma_{\hat E})$. The current draft theorem [[thm-tdmath-regular-energy-shell-measure]] proves the coarea identity, chart independence and positive finite shell mass under its stated $C^2$, compact-regular-band hypotheses; its statement and proof are present, while its acceptance remains unresolved. Multiplying the unnormalized shell measure by a fixed positive phase-volume normalization does not change $\nu_{\hat E}$.

## Definition

Fix a working system $s$ of constitution $c$ and a closed process record $P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cl}}(s)$ with equilibrium endpoints as in [[def-td-process-and-protocol]]. A cycle of the working system is such a record with $x_P^-=x_P^+$; the reservoirs and work store need not return to their initial energy states.

An ideal thermal reservoir $b$ has an energy interval $J_b\subseteq\mathbb R$ measured in joules and a finite entropy function $S_b:J_b\to\mathbb R$ measured in $\mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. On the energy interval admitted for a cycle, assume the exact affine law
$$S_b(E_b)=s_{b,0}+\frac{E_b}{T_b}$$
for a constant $s_{b,0}$ and fixed $T_b>0$ kelvins. Thus $S_b'(E_b)=1/T_b$ in the interior and every admitted endpoint change is exactly $\Delta S_b=\Delta E_b/T_b$. This constant is the absolute thermodynamic temperature under [[def-td-temperature-pressure-chemical-potential]]. The affine entropy law on the admitted interval is the ideal-bath model; a finite reservoir whose temperature changes is outside this definition.

An ideal work store is a named auxiliary with an energy coordinate $E_w$ measured in joules and an assigned entropy $S_w(E_w)=s_w$ constant on the energy interval used by the cycle. It exchanges only mechanical work and no matter or heat. Its energy may change, while its entropy change is zero by this model definition.

A two-reservoir cycle consists of one working-system cycle, two labelled baths $h,c$ at fixed temperatures $T_h,T_c>0$, and the ideal work store. The labels specify the transfer roles below; the general bookkeeping permits equal or reversed positive bath temperatures. In the strictly ordered subfamily $0<T_c<T_h$, call $h$ the hot bath and $c$ the cold bath. The engine-efficiency and refrigerator bounds use this subfamily. No existence of a cycle with prescribed transfer signs is asserted. They lie inside one isolated outer boundary in the sense of [[def-td-system-and-permitted-exchanges]], so the full compound has no external matter or energy transfer. There are no unlisted heat, work, matter, kinetic-energy, or external-potential-energy changes. The admitted process and transfer signs are those of [[def-td-process-and-protocol]].

For use of [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]], the model supplies an admitted closed process record $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ for this full compound. Its two endpoint configurations lie in the declared equilibrium set of that process model, its separately tracked center-of-mass kinetic and external-field potential energies have zero endpoint change, and its endpoint association $\rho_{P_{\mathrm{tot}}}:\{-,+\}\to\mathcal F$ has both values in the same feasible set $\mathcal F$ from that postulate. In the constituent ordering of $\rho_{P_{\mathrm{tot}}}(\pm)$, the working-system state is $x_P^\pm$ and the bath and work-store components have the corresponding energy coordinates $E_h^\pm,E_c^\pm,E_w^\pm$. The total-compound record and the working-system record therefore have matching working-system endpoints; all bath and work-store energy differences below refer to these same total-compound endpoint tuples. The former record is the input to the second-law postulate, and $P$ is the working-system record to which the first-law balance applies.

For each endpoint $\pm$, the model declares the additive entropy split
$$S_{\mathrm{tot}}\!\left(\rho_{P_{\mathrm{tot}}}(\pm)\right)=S_{\mathrm{ws}}(x_P^\pm)+S_h(E_h^\pm)+S_{\mathrm{cold}}(E_c^\pm)+S_w(E_w^\pm),$$
where $S_{\mathrm{ws}}$ is the working-system entropy and the bath and work-store functions are those defined here. This constituent split is assumed to be admitted by [[post-td-concave-fundamental-entropy]] and is the entropy supplied to [[post-td-macroscopic-second-law]]; $S_w$ contributes zero change. When reversibility is asserted, $P_{\mathrm{tot}}$ is reversible relative to its declared outer boundary and protocol as in [[def-td-reversible-process]].

In the heat-engine mode, the positive magnitudes $Q_h,Q_c$ in joules mean respectively heat taken from bath $h$ into the working system and heat rejected by the working system to bath $c$; accordingly $\Delta E_h=-Q_h$, $\Delta E_c=Q_c$, $Q[P]=Q_h-Q_c$, and work output is $W_{\mathrm{out}}=-W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$. The work store gains exactly this transferred work, so $\Delta E_w=W_{\mathrm{out}}$. In the refrigerator mode, $Q_c>0$ is heat taken from bath $c$ into the working system, $Q_h>0$ is heat rejected to bath $h$, so $\Delta E_c=-Q_c$, $\Delta E_h=Q_h$, $Q[P]=Q_c-Q_h$, and work input is $W_{\mathrm{in}}=W_{\mathrm{on}}[P]>0$. The store supplies that work, so $\Delta E_w=-W_{\mathrm{in}}$. These are idealized model conventions, not claims that a particular apparatus realizes the cycle.

## Definition

For the pair potential $\varphi$ of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]], let $B=\{x\in\mathbb R^d:\varphi(x)=+\infty\}$. A finite configuration is hard-admissible if every pair displacement avoids $B$. For $z>0$, define the retained-admissibility zero-inverse-temperature free-wall weight of $\omega$ to be
$$w_0(\omega)=z^{N(\omega)}\mathbf 1_{\{H_{N(\omega)}(\omega)<\infty\}}.$$
Its finite-volume partition sum, when finite, is $\Xi_{\Lambda}^{\mathrm{ret},0}(z)=\sum_{N\geq0}\int w_0(\omega)\,\mu_{\Lambda,N}(d\omega)$, using [[post-td-classical-indistinguishable-particle-measure]]. This definition sets the weight of a forbidden configuration to zero; it does not assign a value to the undefined product $0\cdot(+\infty)$. When $B=\varnothing$ the measure is the unrestricted Poisson activity model; for a nonempty hard core it is generally not Poisson. The convention is explicit model data and carries no statement about an arbitrary zero-width energy shell.

For a periodic cell of side $L$ in dimensionless coordinates, use the exact image energy $H_{L,\mathrm{per}}$ of [[def-td-stable-tempered-continuum-preparation]]. Its periodic retained-admissibility weight is
$$w_{L,0}^{\mathrm{per}}(\omega)=z^{N(\omega)}\mathbf1_{\{H_{L,\mathrm{per}}(\omega)<+\infty\}}=z^{N(\omega)}\mathbf1_{\{\varphi(y-x)<+\infty\text{ for every }x\in\omega,\ y\in\omega^{\mathrm{per}},\ y\ne x\}}.$$
Thus every forbidden pair between distinct particles and every forbidden periodic-image pair, including a particle with one of its own nontrivial images, receives zero weight. When finite, the corresponding partition sum is $\Xi_{L}^{\mathrm{ret},0,\mathrm{per}}(z)=\sum_{N\geq0}\int w_{L,0}^{\mathrm{per}}\,d\mu_{\Lambda_L,N}$. This is the periodic retained-admissibility convention; it is not an unrestricted zero-beta limit of a shell law.

## Definition

Let $I$ be a nonempty finite or countably infinite set equipped with a specified enumeration, let $E_i\in\mathbb R$ be finite energies, let $g_i>0$ be weights, and let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open parameter interval. For a nonnegative family $(a_i)_{i\in I}$ define $\sum_{i\in I}a_i:=\sup_{F\subset I,\,F\text{ finite}}\sum_{i\in F}a_i$, with finite sums as in [[def-finite-sum]] and the supremum as in [[def-complete-ordered-field]] when the finite subsums are bounded; set the value to $+\infty$ when they are unbounded. This definition is independent of the specified enumeration. For $\beta\in J$, define the nonnegative partition sum $Z(\beta):=\sum_{i\in I}g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)$ by this rule. The admissible parameter set is $J_Z:=\{\beta\in J:0<Z(\beta)<\infty\}$. For $\beta\in J_Z$, define $p_i(\beta):=g_i\exp(-\beta E_i)/Z(\beta)$. A countable probability law on $I$ means a nonnegative family with total sum $1$ under the finite-subsum convention above; these weights form such a law because $\sum_i p_i(\beta)=Z(\beta)/Z(\beta)=1$. For any real family $X_i$ with $\sum_i p_i|X_i|<\infty$, define $\langle X\rangle_\beta:=\sum_i p_iX_i$. If $\sum_i|p_i\log(p_i/g_i)|<\infty$, define the reference-relative entropy $H_g(p):=-\sum_i p_i\log(p_i/g_i)$. When $g_i=1$, this is the Shannon entropy with natural logarithms. A lower bound on the energies alone is not part of this definition and does not imply $Z(\beta)<\infty$. For countably infinite $I$, any specified enumeration is used only to write a list; the nonnegative sum itself is the supremum over finite subsums above.

## Scope

The sum is interpreted using the series convention of [[def-series]]. The model is purely mathematical; any physical interpretation of $E_i$, $g_i$, or $\beta$ requires separate premises.

## Definition

Use $\mathbb N$ from [[def-natural-numbers]], which includes $0$, and define $\mathbb N_{>0}:=\mathbb N\setminus\{0\}$. A **finite-state thermodynamic-limit contract** specifies a sequence $(X_k,E_k,g_k,V_k,n_k)_{k\in\mathbb N_{>0}}$, where each $X_k$ is a finite nonempty state set, $E_k:X_k\to\mathbb R$ assigns finite energies in joules, $g_k:X_k\to(0,\infty)$ assigns positive dimensionless weights, $V_k>0$ is physical volume in $\mathrm{m^3}$, and, for one declared species, $n_k>0$ is its amount in moles. A fixed-density sequence has $V_k\to\infty$ and $n_k/V_k\to\rho\in(0,\infty)$ in $\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$. Boundary conditions, interaction rules, and the choice of a volume or amount normalization are part of the contract and must be held fixed or explicitly tracked as $k$ varies.

For $T>0$, set $\beta:=(k_BT)^{-1}$ in $\mathrm{J^{-1}}$, with $k_B$ and units from [[def-td-si-quantities]]. The finite-state canonical partition sum is

$$
Z_k(\beta):=\sum_{x\in X_k}g_k(x)e^{-\beta E_k(x)},
$$

as the finite case of [[def-tdmath-countable-canonical-model]]. It is a positive finite real number. Define $F_k(\beta):=-\beta^{-1}\log Z_k(\beta)$ in joules and $f_k(\beta):=F_k(\beta)/V_k$ in $\mathrm{J\,m^{-3}}$. The specified thermodynamic-limit value is $f(\beta,\rho):=\lim_{k\to\infty} f_k(\beta)$ **if this limit exists**. A limit per mole or per lattice site is a different normalization and must be stated separately.

This is a contract for what a limit claim must specify, not a theorem that the limit exists. It asserts no uniformity in $\beta$, derivative interchange, ensemble equivalence, convergence rate, or nonanalyticity. A finite model's regularity and any limiting singularity require their own arguments; neither is inferred from the word “thermodynamic limit.”

## Definition

Fix integers $d\ge1$, $L\ge1$, a finite alphabet $\mathcal A$ of cardinality $q\ge1$, and a finite, possibly empty, list of interaction shapes $S_a\subset\mathbb Z^d$, each nonempty and contained in $[-R,R]^d$ for some integer $R\ge0$. $\|\Phi_a\|_\infty$ is finite because its domain is finite. ## Statement

For the cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$, $F$ is positively homogeneous, invariant under adding the same catalyst to both endpoints, and satisfies the triangle inequality whenever the extended-real sum on its right is defined. It is subadditive under composition whenever $F(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)+F(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$ is defined. Every pair of actual forward and reverse decorated-chain witnesses has nonnegative total cost. A finite reverse witness therefore bounds all forward costs below; $F=-\infty$ can occur only when the reverse direction has no witness.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A1–A6 on accessible finite compounds, the additive extensive entropy $\sigma$, and the decorated-chain definition.

[A1] [[def-tdmath-forward-sector-hypotheses]]: accessibility is reflexive, transitive, consistent under common spectators, and positively scalable; stability is available.

[F1] [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]]: each chain has a finite real cost, and $F$ is its infimum, with empty infimum $+\infty$.

[F2] [[thm-tdmath-arbitrary-family-calibration]]: $\sigma$ is additive and extensive on every separated finite compound and represents same-type comparisons.

## Proof

1.1 A reflexive identity edge from any nonempty state of $\Gamma$ to itself has cost zero, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)\le0$. For a decorated closed chain, start with the compound containing every edge input $a_0,\ldots,a_{N-1}$. Apply the edge $a_0\prec b_1$ with all other edge inputs as spectators, then apply $a_1\prec b_2$ with the already produced $b_1$ and all still-unused inputs as spectators, and continue through $a_{N-1}\prec b_N$. Consistency and transitivity give $\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}a_k\prec\sum_{k=1}^{N}b_k$. Since $T_N=T_0$ and the intermediate types occur once on each side, these two compounds have the same total type up to the declared reassociation and permutation. Their entropy difference is exactly the chain cost. The same-type entropy representation [F2] makes this difference nonnegative. Hence every closed-chain witness costs at least zero and $F(\Gamma,\Gamma)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.2 Take finite witnesses for $(\Gamma_1,\Gamma'_1)$ and $(\Gamma_2,\Gamma'_2)$. Run the first chain with a fixed state of $\Gamma_2$ and its second catalyst as spectators; then run the second chain with the first chain's output state and first catalyst as spectators. Consistency allows both sequences, and each fixed spectator contributes zero entropy difference. The resulting witness from $\Gamma_1\times\Gamma_2$ to $\Gamma'_1\times\Gamma'_2$ has the sum of the two costs. If both infima are finite real numbers, choose witnesses within $\epsilon/2$ of each infimum and let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. If one infimum is $-\infty$ and the other is finite, use a fixed finite witness for the latter and arbitrarily negative witnesses for the former; the product costs are unbounded below. If both are $-\infty$, choose both costs arbitrarily negative, so the product infimum is $-\infty$. If either is $+\infty$ and the other is not $-\infty$, the right side is $+\infty$ and the inequality is automatic. The mixed extended sum $+\infty+(-\infty)$ is undefined and is excluded by the Statement. [A1, F1, F2, construct]

1.3 A witness for $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$ is a witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$ with enlarged catalyst $C_0\times C$, so $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')\le F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)$. Conversely, add one fixed state of the nonempty catalyst $C_0$ to every edge of an arbitrary witness for $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. Its cost is unchanged, proving the reverse inequality. Thus $F(\Gamma\times C_0,\Gamma'\times C_0)=F(\Gamma,\Gamma')$. [A1, F1, F2]

2.1 Scaling every state, type, and catalyst in a witness by $t>0$ multiplies its cost by $t$ because $\sigma_{tT}(ta)=t\sigma_T(a)$. This gives $F(t\Gamma,t\Gamma')\le tF(\Gamma,\Gamma')$; applying the same argument with scale $1/t$ gives equality, including the extended values. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Concatenate a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma'$ with one from $\Gamma'$ to $\Gamma''$, adding the other chain's fixed catalyst state as spectator to each edge. The result is a witness from $\Gamma$ to $\Gamma''$ whose cost is the sum. Taking finite approximations proves the triangle inequality when both costs are finite; an unbounded-below term with a finite witness in the other direction gives the corresponding $-\infty$ case; if a term is $+\infty$ and the sum is defined, the inequality is automatic. For an actual forward witness and an actual reverse witness with possibly different catalysts, add the reverse catalyst's fixed state to every forward edge and the forward catalyst's fixed state to every reverse edge. Consistency supplies these padded edges, and additivity makes each edge cost unchanged. The padded chains now have the same catalyst, so concatenate them into a closed chain; step 1.1 gives $c+d\ge0$. Thus any fixed finite reverse witness of cost $d$ bounds every forward witness below by $-d$. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, construct] ∎

## Definition

For the type set $\mathcal G$ and cost $F$ of [[def-tdmath-decorated-chain-costs]], define the relation $\Gamma\approx_0\Gamma'$ by $F(\Gamma,\Gamma')=F(\Gamma',\Gamma)=0$. Let $\mathcal P:=\mathcal G\times\mathcal G$ be the set of raw type pairs. Define a relation on raw pairs by
